Amino acid basics

1unlocks 6
A student lists general properties of the amino acids that ribosomes build into human proteins. Which statement is correct?
  1. A. Human proteins contain D- and L-amino acids in roughly equal amounts
  2. B. The α-carbon carries two amino groups, one carboxyl group and an R group
  3. C. All are L-isomers, and glycine is the only one whose α-carbon is not chiral
  4. D. Every standard amino acid has an asymmetric (chiral) α-carbon
  5. E. More than 300 different amino acids are encoded into human proteins
AnswerC. All are L-isomers, and glycine is the only one whose α-carbon is not chiral
WhyThe α-carbon carries an amino group, a carboxyl group, an H and an R group; four different groups make it chiral, and human proteins use L-isomers only. A is the trap: glycine (R = H) has two identical H atoms, so it is achiral. Over 300 amino acids exist in nature, but only 20 are built into proteins.
Key factα-carbon + 4 groups: α-amino (NH3⁺), α-carboxyl (COO⁻), H, and the R side chain (only R differs).
Chirality: 4 different groups → chiral; glycine (R = H) is the only achiral one.
Mammalian proteins use L-isomers only (no D); more than 300 amino acids exist in nature but only 20 are used in proteins.
What it unlocks: 6 questions · 1 you might not expect

Questions you might not expect it to answer (1)

  1. One extra stepQ100 Fischer-type drawing of citrulline from watermelon: is it a D- or L-amino acid, and why?
    Biological amino acids are L: turn the drawing so COO⁻ is on top; the α-NH3+ then points left → L-citrulline, the same configuration as every residue in human proteins.

How it shows up

  • Direct: "which statement is true about amino acids in human proteins?" with L/D, "all chiral" and "over 300" options
  • "Which amino acid is non-chiral because its α-carbon lacks four different groups?" → glycine
  • "Which groups are attached to the α-carbon?" with distractors adding phosphate, aldehyde, hydroxyl or two amino groups
  • Structure drawing (citrulline): D or L? → L, like all biological amino acids

What it lets you eliminate

  • Any option putting D-amino acids in human proteins
  • "All standard amino acids are chiral" (glycine is not) or the reverse, "only glycine is chiral"
  • "More than 300 in human proteins"; an α-carbon with phosphate, aldehyde or two amino/carboxyl groups

Amino acid basics

2unlocks 15
A missense variant changes serine 45 of an enzyme to isoleucine. How is this substitution best described?
  1. A. A hydrophobic residue replaced by a polar one
  2. B. A basic residue replaced by an aromatic one
  3. C. An acidic residue replaced by a hydrophobic one
  4. D. A polar uncharged residue replaced by a hydrophobic one
  5. E. A conservative swap between two hydroxyl-containing residues
AnswerD. A polar uncharged residue replaced by a hydrophobic one
WhySerine (–OH) is polar uncharged (S, T, N, Q) and isoleucine is hydrophobic aliphatic, so this is a nonconservative polar → hydrophobic change. C is the trap: Ile has no hydroxyl; only S, T and Y carry –OH, which is why they are the phosphorylation sites. Ser was never charged, so B and E fail.
Key fact
  • Hydrophobic aliphatic: G, A, V, L, I, M and (in this course) C
  • Hydrophobic aromatic: F, Y, W. Tyr is mainly hydrophobic although its –OH can H-bond; Trp's indole N is not basic
  • Pro: its own class, a cyclic α-imino acid
  • Polar uncharged: S, T, N, Q (form H-bonds). The –OH residues S, T, Y are the phosphorylation sites (Ser most common)
  • Acidic (−): D, E. Basic (+): K, R, H
A conservative substitution stays in one class (Ala→Gly, Gln→Ser); a class change is nonconservative (Thr→Leu polar → hydrophobic; Glu→Val acidic → hydrophobic, as in HbS; Ser→Pro).
Primer 7 puts Cys with the hydrophobic aliphatic residues (q103 keys Cys); some texts call Cys polar. His is listed as basic even though its pKa is about 6.

Questions you might not expect it to answer (1)

  1. Vignette never names itQ112 Adding Gln to a new protein causes toxicity: which amino acid could replace it with minimal side effects?
    'Minimal side effects' = a conservative swap within one class. Gln is polar uncharged → another polar uncharged residue, Ser. Pro kinks, Leu is hydrophobic, Asp acidic, His basic.

How it shows up

  • Mutation vignette (kinase Thr315Leu in CML, Glu→Val) → describe the change in R-group property
  • "Which amino acid is NOT hydrophobic?" (Glu, His) / "hydrophobic and aliphatic?" (Met, Cys) / "hydrophilic and acidic?" (Glu)
  • Tyrosine and tryptophan statements: Tyr has a polar –OH but is classed mainly hydrophobic
  • Conservative vs nonconservative pairs; "which residue could replace Gln with least effect?" (Ser); which residue in a peptide can be phosphorylated (Ser)
  • Dipeptide puzzle: aliphatic N-terminal residue + basic C-terminal residue → Val-His

What it lets you eliminate

  • Tyr or Trp called hydrophilic, charged or basic; Phe given an –OH
  • "Negatively charged → neutral" for Thr or Ser: they were never charged
  • Phosphorylation on Lys, Pro, Ala or Gly (no –OH)
  • "Both conservative" when one swap involves Pro or crosses classes

Charge and pH

3unlocks 15
Which peptide carries a net charge of −1 at pH 7.4?
  1. A. His-Asp-Arg-Ala-Pro
  2. B. Ser-Asp-Gly-Leu-Thr
  3. C. Gly-Tyr-Gln-Asn-Phe
  4. D. Arg-Asp-Glu-Lys-Met
  5. E. Lys-Glu-Ala-Val-Gly
AnswerB. Ser-Asp-Gly-Leu-Thr
WhyThe termini cancel (+1, −1), so only charged side chains count: Asp is the only one in B (−1). In D, Gln and Asn are amides, not acids (0); A and C pair each acid with Lys or Arg (0); in E histidine (pKa about 6) is about 0, so Asp + Arg = 0.
Key factAt pH 7.4 the free termini cancel (N-terminal NH3⁺ +1, C-terminal COO⁻ −1); count side chains only:
  • Asp (D), Glu (E): −1 each
  • Lys (K), Arg (R): +1 each
  • All others: 0 (Gln, Asn, Ser, Thr, Tyr, Cys are uncharged)
His: imidazole pKa about 6 → weakly basic, mostly uncharged at 7.4 (count about 0 in sums; the course still lists it as basic, positive, in classification questions). It is the only side chain with a pKa near 7.4 → the buffering residue of proteins (albumin, Hb) and an active-site acid–base catalyst.
Lys/Arg-rich histones are positive and bind the negative DNA phosphates ionically.
q78 is left out: counting His as about 0, option E (+3) beats the keyed C (+2); counting His as +1 they tie. The lecture slide calls His net positive; the bridge slide treats it as mostly uncharged. No other keyed answer changes with how His is counted.
What it unlocks: 15 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • "What is the net charge of this oligopeptide at pH 7.4?" (often written NH3⁺-…-COO⁻)
  • "Which peptide is net positive / net negative / most basic / most acidic?" across five sequences
  • Single residue: which is negatively charged at 7.4 (Asp); match residues to + or −
  • Histidine: imidazole near-neutral pKa; best buffer at physiological pH (albumin, a His-rich protein); histones bind DNA through positive Lys/Arg

What it lets you eliminate

  • Never count the termini or neutral residues (Gln, Asn, Ser, Thr, Tyr, Cys) as charged
  • Lys, Arg, Asp, Glu, Leu do not buffer at 7.4 (pKa far away): pick His for buffering stems
  • Histone–DNA binding is ionic (positive charge), not hydrophobic methyls, intercalation or covalent bonding

4unlocks 25
Glycine (pK1 = 2.3, pK2 = 9.6) is titrated from pH 1 with NaOH. Which describes the solution after 0.5 equivalent of OH⁻ has been added?
  1. A. pH 2.3; a 50:50 mix of the +1 form and the zwitterion, average charge +½, maximum buffering
  2. B. pH 5.95; almost all glycine is the zwitterion, net charge 0
  3. C. pH 2.3; the steepest part of the curve, with the poorest buffering
  4. D. pH 9.6; half of the amino groups have lost their proton
  5. E. pH 2.3; glycine would migrate toward the anode in an electric field
AnswerA. pH 2.3; a 50:50 mix of the +1 form and the zwitterion, average charge +½, maximum buffering
WhyHalfway to the first equivalence point pH = pK1, so –COOH and –COO⁻ are 50:50: average charge +½ on the flat part of the curve, where buffering is maximal. The steep, poorly buffered points are the equivalence points (1.0 equivalent = pI 5.95; 2.0 = end). Below its pI glycine is net positive, so it moves to the cathode, not the anode.
Key factRule: pH below a group's pKa → it keeps its H⁺; above → it loses it. At 7.4: α-COO⁻ (pKa about 2) and α-NH3⁺ (pKa about 9–10) → zwitterion = equal + and − charges, net 0.
pI = average of the two pKas flanking the zwitterion: 2 groups → (pK1 + pK2)/2 (alanine (2.3 + 9.1)/2 = 5.7); 3 groups → the two nearest: acidic uses the two lowest (Asp = 3.0), basic the two highest (Arg = 10.75). Never average all three.
pH below pI → net + (moves to cathode); above pI → net − (anode); at the pI no migration.
Titration curve: start = fully protonated (+1) → flat midpoint = pK1 (50:50, +½, max buffering) → steep jump at 1st equivalence = pI (zwitterion, 0, poor buffering) → flat = pK2 (half the NH3⁺ deprotonated, −½) → 2nd equivalence = end (−1, poor buffering).
F0666:15 says that above the pI a protein is 'negatively charged (cationic)': the right word is anionic. q99 keys III and V (equivalence points) as the worst buffering regions; the source textbook key may also list point I.

How it shows up

  • At the pI a protein neither moves nor denatures

Peptide bond

5unlocks 9
Which statement about the bond that links residues in a polypeptide is correct?
  1. A. It joins the side chain of one residue to the side chain of the next
  2. B. It is an ester bond formed by hydrolysis
  3. C. The R groups across it are usually cis, and sequences are read from the C-terminus
  4. D. It rotates freely, which gives the chain its flexibility
  5. E. It is an amide bond formed with loss of water; its atoms lie in one plane with R groups usually trans
AnswerE. It is an amide bond formed with loss of water; its atoms lie in one plane with R groups usually trans
WhyThe peptide bond is an amide made by condensation (water out) and cut by hydrolysis. Its partial double-bond character locks the peptide unit flat with R groups trans; the chain's flexibility comes from rotation at the α-carbon (Φ and Ψ), not at the C–N bond, so B is wrong.
Key factPeptide bond = covalent amide link between the α-carboxyl of one residue and the α-amino group of the next, formed by condensation (water released) and broken by hydrolysis (water added).
Partial double-bond character → no rotation about C–N; the peptide unit (Cα and C=O of one residue, N–H and Cα of the next) is planar, R groups usually trans; rotation only about N–Cα (Φ) and Cα–C (Ψ).
Sequences are written and read N-terminal (free amino, left) → C-terminal (free carboxyl, right); n residues are joined by n − 1 peptide bonds.
What it unlocks: 9 questions · 1 you might not expect

Questions you might not expect it to answer (1)

  1. One extra stepQ128 A drawn peptide structure: is it an amino acid, a tripeptide, a tetrapeptide, a lipid or a carbohydrate?
    Count the amide (C=O–NH) links: n residues use n − 1 peptide bonds, so 3 peptide bonds → 4 residues → tetrapeptide, not the tripeptide you get by counting bonds.

How it shows up

  • "Which describes the formation of a peptide bond?" (condensation, amide) or "breaking a peptide bond requires…" (hydrolysis)
  • Peptide unit geometry: coplanar atoms, trans R groups, rotation only at Φ and Ψ
  • Reading a sequence (Tyrosylglycylglycylphenylalanylleucine): free amino N-terminus on the left, free carboxyl C-terminus on the right
  • "What holds amino acids together in a protein?" → peptide bonds; structure drawing → count the residues (tetrapeptide)

What it lets you eliminate

  • Ester, ionic or hydrogen bond as the peptide bond; "formed by hydrolysis"
  • Free rotation about the C–N bond; cis R groups; side chain-to-side chain linkage
  • Reading C → N, or the free amino group on the right

Levels of structure

6unlocks 16
A protein made of a single polypeptide chain is treated with a reducing agent that breaks S–S bonds and nothing else. Which level of structure is directly disrupted?
  1. A. None, because disulfide bonds are non-covalent
  2. B. Primary
  3. C. Secondary
  4. D. Tertiary
  5. E. Quaternary
AnswerD. Tertiary
WhyDisulfide bonds are covalent side-chain cross-links counted in tertiary structure, which uses both non-covalent and covalent interactions. A single-chain protein has no quaternary structure (and subunits are held non-covalently anyway), and primary structure is only the peptide bonds, which a reducing agent leaves intact.
Key fact
  • Primary = the sequence, held by covalent peptide bonds only
  • Secondary = α-helix, β-sheet, turns: backbone H-bonds (C=O to N–H)
  • Tertiary = 3-D fold of one chain: side-chain (R-group) interactions: hydrophobic (the main one), H-bonds, ionic (salt bridges), disulfide (covalent), metal ions (zinc finger) → both non-covalent and covalent
  • Quaternary = two or more chains, held non-covalently (H-bond, ionic, hydrophobic, metal ions): Hb α2β2, insulin hexamer around Zn²⁺. Myoglobin is one chain (no quaternary)
Peptide bonds never stabilize tertiary or quaternary structure.
q118 prints 'secondary structure' for zinc fingers; Primer 8 lists metal-ion complexes (zinc finger) under tertiary, so the lecture answer is C, tertiary. q114: hemoglobin has no disulfide bonds at all; disulfide is keyed only because the course teaches it as tertiary and quaternary as non-covalent. q126 keys side-chain interactions; Lecture 22 also says the primary sequence determines the fold, so A is a tempting alternative.
What it unlocks: 16 questions · 3 you might not expect

Questions you might not expect it to answer (3)

  1. Trap: the obvious answer is wrongQ126 A polypeptide's ability to fold into its 3-D shape depends on what: sequence, side-chain interactions, peptide bonds or random events?
    The 3-D fold is tertiary structure, held by side-chain (R-group) interactions. 'The amino acid sequence' tempts, but that is primary structure, as are peptide bonds → side-chain interactions.
  2. Answered by eliminationQ80 Which pair names the bonds 'within a protein in primary structure'? Each option pairs two bond types.
    Primary = peptide bonds between amino acids; only option a says that, so it wins even though its added C=O···H–N H-bonds belong to secondary structure. The rest lead with non-peptide bonds.
  3. Asked from the other directionQ114 Which bond is absent when Hb α2β2 assembles but present when a single α subunit folds?
    Asked as the difference between levels: quaternary assembly is non-covalent only; tertiary folding adds covalent disulfide bonds. H-bonds, ionic, hydrophobic and metal ions occur in both → disulfide (slide key; real Hb has none).

How it shows up

  • Matching levels to bonds: peptide bonds, H-bonds, disulfide bonds, subunit interactions
  • "Which is NOT involved in tertiary structure?" → peptide bonds; "which is false?" → "tertiary involves only non-covalent interactions"
  • Hb α2β2 or insulin hexamer → quaternary; "what holds quaternary structure?" → non-covalent interactions
  • "Bond present in folding of the Hb α subunit but not in α2β2 assembly" → disulfide (course logic); zinc finger → tertiary; hydrophobic interactions ↔ tertiary

What it lets you eliminate

  • Peptide bonds as a tertiary or quaternary force
  • "Tertiary is only non-covalent"; covalent bonds holding quaternary subunits together
  • Myoglobin (one chain) as a quaternary example; disulfide or salt bridges as primary structure

Used together with

Helix and sheet are both backbone H-bonds; Cysteine cross-links: disulfide and zinc finger

Secondary structure

7unlocks 12TA ×1
Normal prion protein (PrPC, mostly α-helix) refolds into PrPSc (mostly β-sheet) with no change in its amino acid sequence. Which bonds are rearranged in this change?
  1. A. Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups
  2. B. Hydrophobic interactions between nonpolar side chains
  3. C. Ionic bonds between charged side chains
  4. D. Peptide bonds between adjacent residues
  5. E. Disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains
AnswerA. Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups
WhyThe α-helix and the β-sheet are both secondary structure, held by backbone C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds: within one chain (n to n + 4) in the helix, between strands in the sheet. Switching one for the other rearranges those H-bonds. The unchanged sequence shows the peptide bonds are intact; disulfide, ionic and hydrophobic forces are tertiary.
Key factSecondary structure = local folds held by H-bonds between backbone C=O and N–H (not side chains).
α-helix: right-handed, 3.6 residues per turn; the C=O of residue n bonds the N–H of residue n + 4 → intrachain H-bonds running parallel to the axis; R groups point outward.
β-sheet: H-bonds between adjacent strands (separate chains or distant parts of one chain), parallel or antiparallel; R groups above and below the sheet.
A helix ↔ sheet switch (amyloid or prion β-sheet ↔ α-helix) only rearranges these H-bonds; peptide and disulfide bonds are untouched.

Questions you might not expect it to answer (2)

  1. Answered by eliminationQ138 Comparing the α-helix and the β-sheet: which statement is true only for the β-sheet?
    Backbone C=O···N–H H-bonds, globular proteins, secondary and supersecondary structure fit both. Helix H-bonds are always intrachain (n → n + 4); only a sheet joins separate chains → interchain H-bonds.
  2. One extra stepQ131 Drawing of an α-helix segment with atoms labeled A–F: which two would form the helix hydrogen bond?
    Find the C=O oxygen of residue n and the N–H hydrogen of residue n + 4, one turn along; neighbors (n + 1) and side-chain atoms don't count → B and E.

How it shows up

  • Alzheimer vignette: a drug turns a β-sheet protein into α-helix → which interaction is reorganized (hydrogen bonds)
  • TA style: "α-helices and β-sheets are stabilized by hydrogen bonding; which interaction maintains this level?" → H-bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups
  • Fill-in or "true only for the β-sheet": helix H-bonds within the same chain, sheet H-bonds between strands (interchain)
  • α-helix features: 3.6 residues per turn, n to n + 4, R groups outward; labeled-atom figure → the C=O and N–H one turn apart

What it lets you eliminate

  • "β-sheets are held by H-bonds but α-helices are not" (both are)
  • Peptide, disulfide, ionic or hydrophobic bonds as the secondary-structure bond
  • R groups pointing into the helix core; a left-handed helix; H-bond to the adjacent (n + 1) residue

Secondary structure

8unlocks 14
A single-base change in the mRNA of a membrane transporter abolishes one of its α-helical segments. Which amino acid substitution most likely occurred?
  1. A. Glu → Asp
  2. B. Lys → Arg
  3. C. Leu → Pro
  4. D. Val → Ile
  5. E. Ser → Thr
AnswerC. Leu → Pro
WhyProline's side chain loops back onto its own nitrogen: the rigid imino ring fixes the backbone angle and has no N–H to donate to the helix's H-bonds, so a Leu → Pro change kinks and breaks the helix. The other swaps stay within one class (hydrophobic, acidic, basic, hydroxyl), so the helix survives.
Key factProline = cyclic α-imino acid (secondary amino group): its side chain bonds back to its own N, so the rigid ring locks the N–Cα (Φ) bond and leaves no N–H donor → it cannot join the helix H-bond pattern → helix breaker; it kinks the chain, sits in bends and turns and is never inside an α-helix (abundant in collagen).
Any X → Pro change inside a helix (Leu → Pro in Hb Saki; Met → Pro; codon CUC → CCC, since CCN codes Pro) → a destabilized, unstable protein.
Helix formers are small residues such as Ala; bulky aromatic rings (Trp, Tyr, Phe) are found in β-sheets; Gly is too flexible for helices.
F0407:14 says large amino acids destabilize β-sheets, while F0407:12 says residues with large rings (Trp, Tyr, Phe) are often found in β-sheets; the practice questions follow F0407:12. F0407:11 calls proline 'bulkier'; its ring rigidity and missing N–H are the real reasons.
What it unlocks: 14 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Hemoglobin variant vignette (Hb Saki, Leu → Pro at an arrow on a globin helix) → destabilization of β-globin
  • "Which mutation disrupts an α-helix?" given as amino acid swaps (Met → Pro) or as codons (CUC → CCC)
  • "Why is proline a helix breaker?" / "secondary amino group, inserts a kink, high in collagen" → Pro
  • Helix propensity: Ala in helices; Trp, Tyr, Phe in β-sheets; Pro least likely in a helix; "what causes a kink?"

What it lets you eliminate

  • Proline explanations based on charge, disulfide bonds, a guanidinium group, an imidazole or "the smallest R group" (that is glycine)
  • Conservative swaps (Val/Ile/Leu, Glu/Asp, Lys/Arg, Ser/Thr) do not break helices
  • For Leu → Pro in globin: O2-affinity, salt-bridge or altitude effects; the answer is instability

9unlocks 9
A child with recurrent fractures has missense variants that replace glycine with alanine at several positions in the type I collagen triple helix. Why do these changes disrupt the protein?
  1. A. Glycine forms the disulfide bonds that cross-link the three chains
  2. B. Glycine's positive charge forms salt bridges between the chains
  3. C. Glycine's hydroxyl group is the site of hydroxylation
  4. D. Glycine's ring structure puts the needed bends into each chain
  5. E. Only glycine's hydrogen side chain fits in the crowded center of the triple helix
AnswerE. Only glycine's hydrogen side chain fits in the crowded center of the triple helix
WhyCollagen repeats Gly-X-Y; every third residue faces the center of the triple helix, where only glycine's H side chain fits, so even alanine's methyl blocks tight packing. Glycine has no ring (that is proline), no charge and no –OH; the three chains are held by interchain hydrogen bonds, not disulfides.
Key factGlycine: R = H → the smallest, most flexible residue (and the only achiral one).
Collagen = repeating Gly-X-Y (X often Pro, Y hydroxyproline or hydroxylysine); Gly sits at every third position because only its tiny side chain fits the crowded center of the triple helix → tight packing and tensile strength. The three chains are held together by interchain hydrogen bonds (peptide bonds only link residues within a chain).
β-turn (β-bend): a tight U-turn that reverses chain direction for a compact fold, built from Gly (smallest R) + Pro (kink).
What it unlocks: 9 questions

How it shows up

  • "Which amino acid is at every third position?" → glycine; "what bond coils the chains into the fiber?" → hydrogen bonds
  • "Which pair is common in β-bends?" → glycine and proline; "what does a β-turn do?" → reverses direction for a compact structure

What it lets you eliminate

  • Ring or bend (that is proline), charge, hydroxyl or disulfide properties attributed to glycine
  • Peptide or disulfide bonds as what holds the three collagen chains together
  • Turn pairs that lack Gly + Pro (Gly-Leu, Arg-Pro, Ala-Gly, Trp-Phe)

Tertiary forces

10unlocks 6
Hydropathy analysis of a newly cloned protein shows seven separate stretches of about 20 residues, rich in valine, leucine and isoleucine, each predicted to be α-helical. What do these stretches most likely do?
  1. A. Sit in the core of a soluble protein and bind metal ions
  2. B. Span the lipid bilayer as transmembrane helices
  3. C. Sit on the cytosolic surface and phosphorylate tyrosines
  4. D. Sit on the extracellular surface and bind the hormone
  5. E. Bind DNA in the nucleus through zinc fingers
AnswerB. Span the lipid bilayer as transmembrane helices
WhyNonpolar side chains avoid water: in soluble proteins the hydrophobic effect buries them in the core, and in membrane proteins they face the lipid. A helix of about 20 Val/Leu/Ile residues is just long enough to cross the bilayer, and seven of them mark a GPCR such as the TSH receptor. Ligand binding and signalling use the polar loops, not these stretches.
Key factThe hydrophobic effect is the main driving force of folding: nonpolar side chains (Leu, Ile, Val, Phe) cluster in the core, away from water (entropy-driven), so charged and polar residues (Arg, Lys, Asp, Glu) face the surface.
In membrane proteins the same nonpolar residues face the lipid: an α-helix of about 20 hydrophobic residues (Val, Leu, Ile) = one transmembrane segment; seven of them = a GPCR (e.g. the TSH receptor).
What it unlocks: 6 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • TSH receptor / GPCR vignette: seven ~20-residue Val/Leu/Ile helices → spanning the cell membrane (with or without options)

What it lets you eliminate

  • Hydrophobic residues on the surface of a soluble protein; charged residues buried in the core
  • Disulfide, ionic or metal bonds as the main folding force

A mutation that removes one cysteine from the DNA-binding domain of the glucocorticoid receptor stops it from binding its response element. What normally holds this part of the receptor in shape?
  1. A. A Zn²⁺ ion held by cysteine and histidine side chains (zinc finger)
  2. B. A leucine zipper of interlocking leucine side chains
  3. C. A helix-turn-helix held by peptide bonds between subunits
  4. D. Hydrophobic interactions alone, with no metal ion
  5. E. An Fe²⁺ ion held by leucine side chains
AnswerA. A Zn²⁺ ion held by cysteine and histidine side chains (zinc finger)
WhySteroid and nuclear receptors (glucocorticoid, vitamin D) bind DNA with zinc fingers: a Zn²⁺ held by Cys and His side chains, a metal-ion interaction that stabilizes the fold. Cysteine's other job is the disulfide bond, the only covalent folding force. Leucine zippers use no metal.
Key factDisulfide bond: covalent S–S formed by oxidation of two cysteine –SH groups; the only covalent folding force (hydrophobic, H-bond, electrostatic and van der Waals are non-covalent); the two Cys can be far apart in the sequence; common in secreted proteins (insulin, immunoglobulins). A drug that bonds an internal Cys covalently and resists hydrolysis (activated omeprazole on the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase) carries a reactive sulfhydryl → disulfide.
Zinc finger: Zn²⁺ held by Cys and His side chains (a metal-ion complex, a tertiary interaction); the DNA-binding motif of steroid and nuclear receptors (glucocorticoid, vitamin D).
q38: nuclear-receptor zinc fingers are strictly the all-cysteine (Cys4) type; the course and the key use the classic Cys/His description.

How it shows up

  • "Which bond is covalent?" → disulfide; "which side chains form the covalent cross-links of insulin and antibodies?" → Cys –SH
  • Drug vignette: omeprazole forms a hydrolysis-resistant bond with an internal Cys → the drug has a reactive sulfhydryl group

What it lets you eliminate

  • Hydrophobic, hydrogen, electrostatic or van der Waals interactions as "covalent"

Fatty acids

12unlocks 9
Which fatty acid has the lowest melting point?
  1. A. Oleic acid (18:1, cis)
  2. B. Stearic acid (18:0)
  3. C. Lauric acid (12:0)
  4. D. Linoleic acid (18:2, cis)
  5. E. Palmitic acid (16:0)
AnswerD. Linoleic acid (18:2, cis)
WhyMelting point rises with chain length and falls with each cis double bond, because cis kinks stop the chains packing. Linoleic acid (18:2) has the most kinks; the shorter lauric acid (12:0) is still saturated and straight, so it is solid at room temperature.
Key factNaming: 16:0 = 16 carbons, 0 double bonds. Saturated: palmitic 16:0, stearic 18:0. Monounsaturated: palmitoleic 16:1, oleic 18:1. Polyunsaturated (2 or more): linoleic 18:2, linolenic 18:3, arachidonic 20:4.
Melting point ↑ with chain length, ↓ with each cis double bond: cis bonds kink chains → loose packing → liquid oils and more fluid membranes; saturated chains are straight, pack tightly and are solid (tropical coconut and palm oil); trans chains stay nearly straight.
Saturated and trans fats raise coronary risk; oleic acid (olive oil) lowers total and LDL cholesterol and raises HDL.
Chain-length classes: short, fewer than 6 C; medium 6–12 (made by the lactating mammary gland for infants); long 14–22; very long, more than 22 (myelin).

Lipid classes

13unlocks 18
Adipocyte lipid droplets are isolated. Which pair of molecules would be found inside the droplets rather than in the plasma membrane?
  1. A. Phospholipids and free cholesterol
  2. B. Glycogen and free cholesterol
  3. C. Triacylglycerols and cholesteryl esters
  4. D. Phosphatidylserine and sphingomyelin
  5. E. Free fatty acids and glycerol
AnswerC. Triacylglycerols and cholesteryl esters
WhyStorage lipids are neutral: TAG (glycerol + three ester-linked fatty acids) and cholesteryl ester (cholesterol with its OH esterified) have no polar group, so they fill droplets and lipoprotein cores. Free cholesterol keeps its 3-OH, is amphipathic, and sits in membranes with the phospholipids; free fatty acids and glycerol are what TAG breaks down into.
Key factLipids: insoluble in water, soluble in nonpolar solvents; roles: energy store, membranes, signalling, insulation.
Storage lipids are neutral: TAG = glycerol + 3 fatty acids by ester bonds (cut by lipases, not proteases); no charged carboxylate → less water-soluble than free fatty acids; holds most of the body's fatty acids and is the main fuel store (adipose TAG in white and brown fat), not glycogen. Cholesteryl ester = cholesterol's OH esterified to a fatty acid → neutral. Both go to lipid droplets and lipoprotein cores.
Membrane lipids are amphipathic: phospholipids (polar head facing water, tails buried) and free cholesterol, whose single 3-OH sits at the head groups while its rings lie along the tails; cholesterol buffers fluidity (↑ when cold, ↓ when warm).
q191 prints A (liver glycogen); by the lectures the main fuel store is adipose TAG, option B (subcutaneous fat).

Which membrane lipid is built on a backbone other than glycerol?
  1. A. Phosphatidylcholine (lecithin)
  2. B. Platelet-activating factor
  3. C. Phosphatidylinositol
  4. D. Cardiolipin
  5. E. Sphingomyelin
AnswerE. Sphingomyelin
WhySphingomyelin is a sphingolipid: sphingosine with an amide-linked fatty acid (ceramide) plus phosphocholine. PC, PI, cardiolipin and PAF are all glycerophospholipids; lecithin shares sphingomyelin's phosphocholine head but sits on glycerol.
Key factGlycerophospholipids: glycerol-3-phosphate with 2 fatty acids in ester bonds at C1 and C2 (unsaturated at C2) and a charged head at C3; derivatives of phosphatidic acid. Most abundant: PC, PE, PS; PC = lecithin. PI, cardiolipin and PAF belong here too (and TAG is glycerol-based).
Sphingolipids: backbone = sphingosine (an amino alcohol), NOT glycerol; one fatty acid joined by an amide bond → ceramide; head groups are added to ceramide.
  • Sphingomyelin = ceramide + phosphocholine (taken from lecithin): the only significant sphingophospholipid; myelin
  • Cerebroside (ceramide + one sugar), globoside, ganglioside (GM2): glycosphingolipids with no phosphate → not phospholipids
The defining difference between the two classes is the backbone.
F0381:19's heading calls ceramide 'an ester between a fatty acid and sphingosine', and q220 keys that wording; the bond is an amide, as the same slide's text says. q220 is still answered by recognizing the ceramide option.

A newly imported mitochondrial matrix protein is enclosed in a barrel-shaped, ATP-dependent complex capped by a lid protein, where it folds in isolation. Which protein forms this barrel?
  1. A. Ubiquitin
  2. B. Peptidyl transferase
  3. C. Signal recognition particle
  4. D. Hsp60
  5. E. Hsp70
AnswerD. Hsp60
WhyHsp60 (a chaperonin, with Hsp10 as the lid) is the barrel that folds proteins, mainly in mitochondria. Hsp70 is the tempting choice: it is the most abundant chaperone, but it binds exposed hydrophobic stretches and holds proteins unfolded for translocation rather than enclosing them.
Key factChaperones = heat shock proteins (HSPs): recognize exposed hydrophobic regions of new or misfolded proteins and help them fold correctly; they hydrolyze ATP (ATPase domain); induced by stress.
  • Hsp70: the most abundant chaperone; binds and stabilizes hydrophobic regions, keeping proteins unfolded until they reach their destination (translocation).
  • Hsp60 (chaperonin, + Hsp10 lid): barrel that encloses the protein and folds it, contacting it through hydrophobic (not hydrophilic) patches; main site mitochondria.
  • Proteins chaperones cannot rescue are tagged with ubiquitin → proteasome (e.g., ΔF508 CFTR); enhancing this pathway clears toxic aggregates. Failed chaperone folding underlies misfolding diseases such as Alzheimer.

  1. Looks like another topicQ336 Elderly patient with memory loss; biopsy shows tangles and amyloid plaques: which molecular process is most directly implicated?
    Plaques + tangles are misfolded aggregates, and chaperones (HSPs) are what normally prevent misfolding → impaired chaperone-mediated folding. Ubiquitination is the cleanup step, not the folding failure.
  2. Asked from the other directionQ417 Investigational Parkinson drug lowers toxic mutant protein aggregates in cells: what is its likely mechanism?
    Proteins chaperones cannot rescue get ubiquitin → proteasome, so boosting that clears aggregates → enhances the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. More β-sheet, blocking HSP binding or blocking the native fold all worsen aggregation.
  3. Asked from the other directionQ489 Same Parkinson drug question, options reordered: drug reduces toxic mutant protein aggregates; most likely mechanism?
    Failed-folding proteins go ubiquitin → proteasome; enhancing it lowers aggregate load → enhances the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. Every other option promotes misfolding.

AnswerC. Parkinson disease – α-synuclein
WhyParkinson = α-synuclein (Lewy bodies). Every other option swaps a protein between diseases: amyloid-β is Alzheimer, SOD1 is ALS, huntingtin (polyQ) is Huntington.
Key factMisfolded proteins tend to form β-sheet-rich amyloid fibrils and aggregates:
  • Alzheimer: amyloid-β (cleaved from APP; normal sequence, misfolded) → extracellular β-sheet plaques + intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau tangles. ApoE4 = risk (more plaques), ApoE2 = protective. Therapy idea: slow Aβ aggregation.
  • Parkinson: α-synuclein (Lewy bodies).
  • Huntington: expanded CAG → polyglutamine tract in huntingtin → misfolding and aggregation, a toxic gain of function (autosomal dominant; midlife chorea, personality change).
  • ALS: SOD1.

A pathologist cuts a finger during the autopsy of a patient who died of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. What kind of agent could transmit the disease?

  3. C. A DNA virus

WhyPrions are infectious proteins without nucleic acid: PrPSc has the same amino acid sequence as normal PrPC but a different fold, and it templates normal PrP into more PrPSc. A virus is the tempting answer only because the disease is transmissible.
Key factPrion = misfolded form of a normal host protein (PrP).
  • Same amino acid sequence, different conformation: α-helix → β-sheet, a change in secondary structure.

  • Diseases: Creutzfeldt-Jakob (sporadic, familial, iatrogenic: cadaver tissue, growth hormone), mad cow, kuru (New Guinea cannibalism), scrapie. Rapidly progressive dementia (death within about a year), spongiform vacuolated neurons.

Which property belongs to globular proteins such as hemoglobin rather than to fibrous proteins such as collagen?
  1. A. Irregular amino acid sequence and greater sensitivity to heat and pH
  2. B. Repetitive amino acid sequence

  4. D. Long and narrow shape

AnswerA. Irregular amino acid sequence and greater sensitivity to heat and pH
WhyGlobular proteins are rounded, soluble, functional (transport, catalysis), with irregular sequences, and are more sensitive to heat and pH. The other four options all describe fibrous proteins.
Key fact
  • Fibrous (collagen, keratin, elastin, myosin, actin, fibrin): long and narrow; structural (strength, support); insoluble; repetitive sequence; less sensitive to heat and pH.
  • Globular (hemoglobin, catalase, insulin, immunoglobulins, enzymes): rounded and compact; functional (transport, catalysis); soluble; irregular sequence; more sensitive to heat and pH.
  • So fibrous-protein defects weaken tissues (lax joints, fragile vessels); globular-protein defects lose function (anemia, hypoxia).

Myoglobin vs hemoglobin

Which statement correctly contrasts myoglobin with hemoglobin?
  1. A. Myoglobin has a sigmoidal curve; hemoglobin has a hyperbolic curve
  2. B. Myoglobin is a tetramer with four hemes; hemoglobin is a monomer with one
  3. C. They differ mainly in secondary and tertiary structure
  4. D. Hemoglobin binds O2 with higher affinity than myoglobin
  5. E. Myoglobin is a muscle monomer that stores O2 with higher affinity (lower P50) and a hyperbolic curve
AnswerE. Myoglobin is a muscle monomer that stores O2 with higher affinity (lower P50) and a hyperbolic curve
WhyMyoglobin: monomer, one heme, in muscle, stores O2, high affinity (P50 about 1 mm Hg), hyperbolic. Hemoglobin: tetramer, four hemes, in RBCs, transports O2, P50 about 26 mm Hg, sigmoidal. They share their primary-to-tertiary fold and differ in quaternary structure, so E is the trap.
Key fact
  • Myoglobin: monomer (~17 kDa), 1 heme, 1 O2; cardiac and skeletal muscle; O2 storage for ATP generation during contraction; hyperbolic curve; higher affinity (P50 ≈ 1 mm Hg); no cooperativity.
  • Hemoglobin: tetramer (~64 kDa; 2 α-like + 2 β-like), 4 hemes, 4 O2; in RBCs; O2 transport lungs → tissues; sigmoidal (cooperative); lower affinity (P50 ≈ 26 mm Hg).
  • Similar primary, secondary and tertiary structure; they differ in quaternary structure. Both use Fe2+ heme. In tissues O2 passes from Hb to Mb.

Key fact
  • Heme = Fe2+ in protoporphyrin; only Fe2+ binds O2 (Fe3+ = methemoglobin).
  • Proximal His (F8) binds the iron (5th position); O2 binds the 6th position; distal His (E7) sits on the O2 side. Each subunit's heme binds its own O2.
  • Heme proteins and roles: Hb and Mb = reversible O2 binding; cytochromes = electron transport (Fe2+/Fe3+ cycling); catalase = breaks down H2O2.
q457 is keyed C (catalase), but statement A (heme proteins contain heme as a tightly bound cofactor) is also essentially true.

A mutant hemoglobin tetramer binds O2 at every heme, but O2 binding at one subunit no longer changes the affinity of the others. Its O2-binding curve will most resemble which?
  1. A. Sigmoidal and shifted left
  2. B. Flat, binding no O2
  3. C. Sigmoidal and shifted right, with better unloading
  4. D. Hyperbolic like myoglobin, with poor unloading to tissues
  5. E. The normal hemoglobin curve
AnswerD. Hyperbolic like myoglobin, with poor unloading to tissues
WhyThe sigmoidal shape comes from positive cooperativity. Without it the tetramer behaves like four myoglobins: hyperbolic, high affinity, little O2 released at tissue PO2. A shifted sigmoid is the trap; shifts come from effectors, not from losing cooperativity.
Key fact
  • Positive cooperativity: O2 binding to one subunit shifts the tetramer from T toward R and raises the affinity of the remaining subunits, so affinity increases as saturation rises → sigmoidal curve.
  • Requires quaternary structure (4 interacting subunits); monomeric Mb cannot cooperate → hyperbolic. Lose cooperativity → hyperbolic, poor unloading.
  • Payoff: the steep middle releases a lot of O2 over the tissue PO2 range; the flat top protects loading (alveolar PO2 104 → 60 mm Hg drops saturation only 97% → 89%).

T and R states: shifting the curve

23unlocks 15
Which of the following shifts the hemoglobin–O2 dissociation curve to the LEFT?
  1. A. Decreased pH
  2. B. Strenuous exercise
  3. C. Carbon monoxide poisoning
  4. D. Increased 2,3-BPG
  5. E. Fever
AnswerC. Carbon monoxide poisoning
WhyCO locks the tetramer in the high-affinity R state → left shift. Exercise, ↑2,3-BPG, fever and ↓pH all stabilize the T state → right shift.
Key factT (taut) = deoxy, low affinity; R (relaxed) = oxy, high affinity.
  • Right shift (stabilize T, unload O2): ↑H+ (↓pH), ↑CO2, ↑2,3-BPG, ↑temperature → exercise, altitude adaptation, acidosis, shock.
  • Left shift (stabilize R, hold O2): ↑O2 itself, CO, ↓H+ (↑pH, alkalosis), ↓CO2 (hyperventilation), ↓2,3-BPG, ↓temperature, HbF (α2γ2).

  3. One extra stepQ399 Four temperature/pH pairs: which combination minimizes O2 unloading to tissue?

WhyA right shift means lower affinity, so a higher PO2 is needed for 50% saturation: ↑P50 and easier unloading. Carrying capacity depends on how much Hb there is, so a shift never changes it.
Key fact

  • Left shift = ↑affinity = ↓P50 = harder unloading (R state).
  • O2-binding capacity (≈1.34 mL O2 per g Hb) is not changed by curve shifts or by PO2.

The Bohr effect and CO2

25unlocks 14TA ×2
During vigorous exercise, CO2 and H+ rise in skeletal muscle capillaries. What happens to hemoglobin there?
  1. A. Increased H+ stabilizes the T state, lowering O2 affinity and releasing O2
  2. B. CO2 binds the heme iron and displaces O2
  3. C. Increased pH stabilizes the R state, promoting O2 release
  4. D. Decreased pH increases hemoglobin's O2 affinity
  5. E. H+ prevents hemoglobin from releasing O2
AnswerA. Increased H+ stabilizes the T state, lowering O2 affinity and releasing O2
WhyBohr effect: H+ (made from CO2 by carbonic anhydrase) protonates Hb side chains (histidine) and stabilizes T → right shift → O2 is released where metabolism is high. CO2 binds globin N-terminal amino groups, never the heme iron.
Key fact
  • Bohr effect = Hb O2 affinity falls as pH falls and CO2 rises (temperature shifts the curve too, but it is not part of the Bohr effect).
  • Tissues: CO2 → carbonic acid → H+ binds histidines (pKa near blood pH), and CO2 forms carbamino-Hb → both stabilize T → right shift → O2 unloading.
  • Lungs (higher pH, lower CO2): the reverse → R → left shift → O2 loading.
  • Reciprocal: H+ binding lowers O2 affinity, and O2 binding lowers H+ affinity (oxyHb releases H+; deoxyHb is the better buffer). H+ and O2 bind different sites.
What it unlocks: 16 questions · 2 you might not expect

    Reciprocal Bohr: O2 binding lowers H+ affinity, so oxygenation reduces buffering capacity. 'More histidines' is the trap: the number is fixed, only their pKa changes.
  2. Asked from the other directionQ481 Which statement about the Bohr effect is INCORRECT (proton effect, CO2, O2 effect on H+ affinity, high pH, separate sites)?
    Bohr runs both ways: H+ lowers O2 affinity and O2 binding lowers H+ affinity, so 'O2 binding increases affinity for H+' is the wrong statement.

How it shows up

  • Exercise or sprinter vignette → ↑CO2 and H+ → T state → more O2 release
  • 'Carbon dioxide facilitates O2 release by?' → potentiating the Bohr effect

  • 'Which statement about the Bohr effect is INCORRECT?' → 'O2 binding increases Hb's affinity for H+'; 'which amino acid accepts H+?' → histidine; 'which factors make up the Bohr effect?' → low pH, high CO2

What it lets you eliminate

  • Cross out any pairing of ↓pH with R state, left shift or ↑affinity, and 'Bohr effect occurs only in the lungs'.
  • If asked strictly for Bohr factors, choose low pH + high CO2 without temperature.

A free diver hyperventilates before a dive and blacks out underwater. What did the hyperventilation do to O2 delivery to the tissues?

In venous blood carrying CO2 from the tissues to the lungs, which event occurs?
  1. A. H+ is buffered mainly by oxyhemoglobin
  2. B. The red cells become alkaline

  4. D. HCO3− moves into red cells in exchange for Cl−

WhyIn the RBC, carbonic anhydrase catalyzes CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3−. H+ is buffered by deoxyHb, HCO3− leaves the cell in exchange for Cl− (chloride shift), and it is CO2, not HCO3−, that binds Hb as carbamino-Hb.
Key fact
  • Tissue RBC: carbonic anhydrase CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3−.
  • H+ is buffered by deoxyHb (Bohr), so venous pH falls only slightly.
  • HCO3− exits to plasma in exchange for Cl− (chloride shift) → most CO2 travels as HCO3− in plasma.
  • Some CO2 binds globin N-terminal amino groups = carbaminohemoglobin → stabilizes T, promotes O2 unloading.
  • Lungs: everything reverses (reverse chloride shift) and CO2 is exhaled.

Fetal and adult hemoglobins

33unlocks 4TA ×2
Which sequence correctly shows the normal progression of hemoglobin from embryo to adult?
  1. A. α2γ2 → ζ2ε2 → α2β2
  2. B. α2δ2 → α2γ2 → α2β2
  3. C. ζ2ε2 → α2β2 → α2γ2
  4. D. ζ2γ2 → α2β2 → α2δ2
  5. E. ζ2ε2 → α2γ2 → α2β2
AnswerE. ζ2ε2 → α2γ2 → α2β2
WhyEmbryonic Hb Gower (ζ2ε2, yolk sac) → HbF α2γ2 (liver and marrow from about week 5) → HbA α2β2, which takes over in the months after birth. α2δ2 is HbA2, a minor adult form.
Key fact
  • Two gene families: α-like (ζ, α1, α2; chromosome 16; 4 α genes) and β-like (ε, Gγ, Aγ, δ, β; chromosome 11). Every Hb has 2 α-like + 2 β-like chains.
  • Switching: Gower ζ2ε2 → HbF α2γ2 → HbA α2β2; so β-chain diseases appear only months after birth.
  • Normal adult: HbA (α2β2) ≈ 90%+ (most abundant), HbA2 (α2δ2) 2–3%, HbF (α2γ2) <2%, HbA1c 4–6% (glycated HbA).
Lecture slide 28 says HbA synthesis begins at ~8 months (meaning gestation); HbA becomes predominant after birth. q508's explanation says HbF is under 1% of adult Hb; the lecture says under 2%.

Carbon monoxide

35unlocks 12
Which statement about carbon monoxide's effect on hemoglobin is NOT true?
  1. A. It makes the remaining heme sites bind O2 with lower affinity
  2. B. It makes the curve more hyperbolic
  3. C. It shifts hemoglobin toward the relaxed (R) state
  4. D. It binds heme Fe2+ about 220 times more tightly than O2
  5. E. It shifts the O2-binding curve to the left
AnswerA. It makes the remaining heme sites bind O2 with lower affinity
WhyCO on one heme pushes the tetramer to R, so the remaining hemes hold O2 more tightly (left shift, hyperbolic) and do not unload. That double hit (fewer sites plus no release) is why 50% COHb kills while a 50% anemia does not.
Key fact
  • CO binds heme Fe2+ ~220× (sources say 200–250×) more avidly than O2; binding is reversible.
  • Hit 1: occupies sites → ↓O2 content and saturation (curve plateau lowered).
  • Hit 2: shifts Hb to R → remaining O2 held tightly → left shift, curve becomes hyperbolic → little release to tissues.
  • So 50% COHb is fatal but a 50% anemia is not (the remaining normal Hb still unloads). CO binds Mb too, but Hb cooperativity makes delivery especially impaired.
Lecture gives 220×; some faculty answers say 240× or 210–250×.

A forklift operator working in a closed cold-storage room develops headache, confusion and a seizure. HR 120, RR 30, pulse oximetry 99%. The forklift is propane-powered. Which toxin is most likely?
  1. A. Cyanide
  2. B. Nitrite
  3. C. Carbon dioxide
  4. D. 2,4-Dinitrophenol
  5. E. Carbon monoxide
AnswerE. Carbon monoxide
WhyIncomplete combustion in an enclosed space (propane engine or lantern, car in a garage, house fire, heavy indoor smoking) makes CO. Standard pulse oximetry reads COHb as oxyHb, so 99% is falsely reassuring. CO2, the product of complete combustion, is the classic distractor.
Key fact
  • Source: incomplete combustion in a closed space: propane forklift or lantern, running car in a garage, house fire, indoor smoking.
  • Clues: headache, dizziness, nausea, irritability, confusion, seizure, tachycardia, tachypnea, cherry-red skin; pulse oximetry falsely normal (COHb counted as oxyHb); elevated carboxyhemoglobin; lactic acidosis.
  • Mechanism (3 parts): ↓O2 delivery (COHb, left shift), ↓O2 utilization (CO binds Fe2+ of complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase), and ROS with lipid peroxidation. Brain and heart (highest O2 demand) are hit first.
What it unlocks: 20 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Richard F. case (propane forklift): source? mechanism? systems affected? → CO from forklift fumes; brain, heart, lungs
  • Closed tent with a propane lantern → carbon monoxide (distractors CO2, nitrite, nitrate, thiosulfate, methanol)
  • House fire with elevated carboxyHb and metabolic acidosis; couple who smoke indoors and improve on 100% O2 → carboxyhemoglobin
  • 'Mechanism of toxicity?' → impaired delivery, impaired utilization and ROS (all of the above); 'what did the patient present with?' → normal O2 saturation

What it lets you eliminate

  • Cross out CO2 (complete combustion), thiosulfate and nitrite (cyanide antidotes), and rotenone, DNP or oligomycin (no exposure source).
  • A normal pulse oximeter reading never rules out CO.

A worker recovers in the ER after several hours of breathing 100% O2 for a workplace exposure. Why does this treatment work if the toxin is carbon monoxide?
  1. A. CO is a noncompetitive inhibitor that O2 cannot displace
  2. B. O2 reduces Fe3+ heme back to Fe2+
  3. C. O2 converts CO to CO2 in the blood
  4. D. CO binds the same heme site reversibly, so high O2 competes it off and shortens the COHb half-life
  5. E. O2 shifts the curve to the left, releasing O2 to tissues
AnswerD. CO binds the same heme site reversibly, so high O2 competes it off and shortens the COHb half-life
WhyCO and O2 compete for the same Fe2+ heme site, and CO is not covalently bound, so it is a competitive, reversible inhibitor: flooding with 100% O2 (hyperbaric if severe) displaces it. Reducing Fe3+ is methylene blue's job in methemoglobinemia.
Key fact
  • CO = competitive inhibitor (same heme site on Hb and on complex IV), reversible (noncovalent).
  • Treatment: 100% O2; hyperbaric O2 if severe (seizure, coma). COHb half-life ≈ 4–6 h on room air → ≈ 80 min on 100% O2 → ≈ 20 min hyperbaric.
  • Not CO treatment: nitrites and thiosulfate (cyanide), methylene blue (metHb), CO2 rebreathing, ferrous sulfate, hyperventilation.

A worker exposed to nitrites has cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental O2. Which value is most likely normal?
  1. A. Arterial O2 content
  2. B. O2-carrying capacity of arterial blood
  3. C. Arterial PO2
  4. D. O2 delivery to peripheral tissue
  5. E. Bound fraction (saturation) of arterial O2
AnswerC. Arterial PO2
WhyPaO2 measures only O2 dissolved in plasma, set by lung gas exchange, which is intact. Methemoglobin (like COHb) cannot carry O2, so saturation, content, capacity and delivery fall. Extra O2 raises PaO2 but not the Hb-bound O2.
Key fact
  • PaO2 = dissolved O2 (alveolar gas exchange). Saturation = % of heme sites holding O2. Content ≈ 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 (plus a tiny dissolved part).
  • CO poisoning and methemoglobinemia: PaO2 (and alveolar PO2) normal; true SaO2, content and delivery ↓; supplemental O2 raises PaO2 but does not fix the cyanosis of metHb.
  • Anemia: PaO2 and saturation normal, content ↓. Low V/Q, shunt and hypoventilation lower PaO2 itself.
  • Raising PO2 raises % saturation; raising Hb raises content, not % saturation; neither PO2 nor curve shifts change binding capacity per gram.
What it unlocks: 11 questions · 7 you might not expect

Questions you might not expect it to answer (7)

  1. Trap: the obvious answer is wrongQ513 Which lowers Hb's O2-binding capacity: lower Hb concentration, PaO2 60, PaO2 120, or a left shift?
    Capacity is per gram of Hb (≈1.34 mL/g). Less Hb lowers content, PO2 and shifts change saturation → none of them. 'Less Hb' is the trap.
  2. Trap: the obvious answer is wrongQ409 Percent Hb saturation will increase if: PCO2 up, Hb concentration up, temperature up, PO2 up, or pH down?
    More Hb raises content, not % saturation (the trap). Higher PCO2, heat and acid shift right and lower it → arterial PO2 increased.

  4. Vignette never names itQ253Q445 Worker exposed to nitrites; cyanosis not corrected by O2: which value is most likely normal (content, capacity, PaO2, bound fraction, delivery)?

A 4-month-old has cyanosis, dyspnea and lethargy. Drawn blood is chocolate-brown, and testing shows more hemoglobin with oxidized (Fe3+) iron. Which is the diagnosis?
  1. A. β-Thalassemia major
  2. B. Methemoglobinemia
  3. C. Sickle cell anemia
  4. D. Carbon monoxide poisoning
  5. E. Iron deficiency anemia
AnswerB. Methemoglobinemia
WhyFe3+ heme cannot bind O2 = methemoglobin: cyanosis not corrected by O2 and chocolate-brown blood. CO poisoning keeps the iron Fe2+ and gives cherry-red, not brown, blood.
Key fact
  • Methemoglobin = heme iron oxidized Fe2+ → Fe3+ → cannot bind O2.
  • Causes: oxidizing drugs and chemicals: nitrites/nitrates (isosorbide dinitrate, nitroglycerin, contaminated water), local anesthetics (benzocaine), nitroprusside; or inherited NADH–methemoglobin reductase deficiency or HbM (lifelong cyanosis that runs in families).
  • Signs: cyanosis unresponsive to O2, chocolate-brown blood, headache, anxiety, dyspnea; PaO2 normal.
  • Treatment: methylene blue (reduces Fe3+ → Fe2+ via the reductase).
  • Made on purpose: nitrites create metHb, which binds cyanide (cyanmethemoglobin) and pulls it off complex IV, then thiosulfate. Cyanide = O2 delivered but not used; CO = O2 not delivered (100% O2).

A 30-year-old of Greek descent with mild microcytic anemia has HbA2 of 5% and HbF of 2% on electrophoresis. Which diagnosis is most likely?
  1. A. β-Thalassemia minor
  2. B. Iron deficiency anemia
  3. C. Hemoglobin C disease
  4. D. Sickle cell trait
  5. E. α-Thalassemia trait
AnswerA. β-Thalassemia minor
WhyThalassemia = reduced synthesis of a normal chain. With too little β, the spare α chains pair with δ and γ, so HbA2 (α2δ2) and HbF (α2γ2) rise: β-thalassemia. α-Thalassemia and sickle trait do not raise HbA2.
Key fact
  • Thalassemia = quantitative hemoglobinopathy: ↓synthesis of α or β chains → chain imbalance; autosomal recessive; microcytic, hemolytic. (Qualitative = structurally abnormal chain: HbS, HbC.)
  • β-thal: excess unpaired α chains aggregate and precipitate → premature erythroid cell death.
  • Labs: ↑HbA2 (α2δ2) and ↑HbF (α2γ2), because neither contains β.
  • Minor (β+/β or β0/β): mild microcytic anemia. Intermedia (β+/β+ or β+/β0). Major, Cooley (β0/β0): no HbA, severe anemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities, regular transfusions → iron overload → iron chelators. Mediterranean, Asian, Middle Eastern.

    Normal HbA2 is 2–3%, so 5% is raised; ↑HbA2 + slightly ↑HbF with no symptoms → β-thalassemia minor. α-thal doesn't raise HbA2.

Which correctly describes the mutations of hemoglobin S and hemoglobin C?
  1. A. HbS: Val→Glu; HbC: Lys→Glu, both at β6
  2. B. HbS: Glu→Val; HbC: Glu→Lys, both at position 6 of β-globin
  3. C. Both reduce β-globin synthesis
  4. D. HbS: Glu→Lys; HbC: Glu→Val, both at β6
  5. E. Both are α-globin mutations
AnswerB. HbS: Glu→Val; HbC: Glu→Lys, both at position 6 of β-globin
WhyBoth are single-base missense changes at β6 that replace negatively charged glutamate: HbS → valine (hydrophobic, polymerizes) and HbC → lysine (charged, crystallizes, no sickling). Reversing the direction (Val→Glu) is the most common trap.
Key fact
  • HbS: β-globin (HBB) codon 6 GAG → GTG, Glu → Val (E6V); a missense point mutation (mRNA level and size normal, protein function altered); HbSS = both β chains mutant; autosomal recessive (about 1 in 500 African Americans).
  • HbC: β6 Glu → Lys (charged, hydrophilic) → no hydrophobic patch, no polymerization; forms crystals → mild chronic hemolytic anemia without pain crises. HbSC = milder sickle disease.
  • Not: ΔF508 phenylalanine deletion (CF), α-chain changes, nonsense, frameshift or deletion (would change mRNA or truncate), reduced synthesis (thalassemia).
Lecture slides F1269:35, :40 and :42 print HbC as 'E6L'; the correct change, used by every practice and TA key, is E6K (Glu→Lys). q567's stem says 'microcytic, hypochromic', which fits thalassemia better than sickle cell; the keyed answer (point mutation) is unaffected.

What is the primary structural consequence of the β6 Glu→Val substitution?
  1. A. Formation of α4 tetramers
  2. B. Oxidation of heme iron to Fe3+
  3. C. Polymerization of deoxyHbS through hydrophobic contacts between molecules
  4. D. Increased affinity of the 2,3-BPG pocket
  5. E. Decreased O2 binding by each heme
AnswerC. Polymerization of deoxyHbS through hydrophobic contacts between molecules
WhyValine forms a hydrophobic protrusion that docks into a hydrophobic pocket on another HbS molecule, exposed only in deoxy (T) Hb, so deoxyHbS polymerizes into rigid fibers that sickle the RBC. O2 binding and BPG handling are essentially normal; Fe3+ is methemoglobin.
Key fact
  • Val at β6 = sticky hydrophobic patch → binds a hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring deoxy HbS → deoxyHbS aggregates and polymerizes into insoluble rope-like fibers (↑hydrophobic interactions; quaternary and secondary structure and O2 binding essentially unchanged).
  • Fibers distort RBCs into sickles → vaso-occlusion (ischemia, microinfarcts, pain crises in bone, chest, abdomen) and chronic hemolytic anemia (fragile cells destroyed early, removed by the spleen; jaundice).
  • Case-session summary: deoxyHbS aggregates, mutant β chains sticky, vascular occlusion, chronic anemia, periodic pain.

How can acidosis precipitate a crisis in a patient with sickle cell disease?
  1. A. It decreases 2,3-BPG binding to HbS
  2. B. It favors the R form of HbS
  3. C. It shifts the O2 curve to the left
  4. D. It increases hemoglobin's O2 affinity
  5. E. It decreases the solubility of HbS by favoring the deoxy (T) state
AnswerE. It decreases the solubility of HbS by favoring the deoxy (T) state
WhyAcid → Bohr effect → more HbS in the deoxy T state, which is far less soluble and polymerizes. Every other option runs the Bohr effect backward.
Key fact
  • Only deoxy (T) HbS polymerizes, so anything that stabilizes T or lowers saturation increases sickling: hypoxia (altitude, exertion, lung disease), acidosis, ↑2,3-BPG, ↑CO2.
  • Anything that favors R (more O2, even the first O2 bound) decreases sickling.
  • Acidosis → ↓solubility of HbS (not ↑affinity, not R, not a left shift).

A patient with sickle cell disease flies to Denver and has a pain crisis after a night of heavy drinking. Which best explains how the drinking contributed?

WhyAlcohol is a diuretic → dehydration → higher [HbS] inside RBCs (faster polymerization) and ↑blood viscosity → sickled cells stick and occlude vessels. Denver's PO2 is lower, and the labs show metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis.
Key fact
  • High altitude (Denver, 5,300 ft) → PO2 17–20% lower → more HbS in the deoxy T state → polymerization.

  • Alcohol metabolism → lactic acid → acidosis → T state (the case labs: high anion gap metabolic acidosis, AG 21; tachypnea is compensation).
  • Common triggers: dehydration, infection (the earlier influenza crisis), high altitude, strenuous exercise, cold or heat, smoking, stress.

Arterial pH falls from 7.4 to 6.4. Which change in hydrogen ion concentration has occurred?
  1. A. [OH−] rose tenfold
  2. B. [H+] doubled
  3. C. [H+] rose tenfold
  4. D. [H+] fell tenfold
  5. E. [H+] rose by a factor of 7.4/6.4
AnswerC. [H+] rose tenfold
WhypH = −log[H+], so each 1-unit fall in pH is a 10-fold rise in [H+] (2 units = 100-fold). The ratio of the pH numbers (7.4/6.4) is the usual trap: the scale is logarithmic, and a lower pH means more H+, not less.
Key factpH = −log[H+]: lower pH = higher [H+].
1 pH unit = 10× [H+]; 2 units = 100×; about 0.3 unit = 2×.
Pure water: [H+] = [OH−] = 10⁻⁷ M, so pH 7. Normal blood [H+] is about 40 nM (pH 7.4).

Which statement about acids in water is correct?

The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation applies only to weak acids and bases.

A weak acid HA has a pKa of 5.4. At pH 7.4, what is the ratio [HA] : [A−]?

pH above pKa → more A−; pH below pKa → more HA.

A drug is a weak base with a pKa of 9.0. It enters cells only by diffusing in its uncharged form. At which pH does it cross most readily?

WhyMembranes pass the uncharged form. For a weak base, uncharged B dominates when pH is above pKa; below it the drug is BH+ (charged). Only 9.2 is above 9.0. For a weak acid it is the reverse: uncharged HA dominates below pKa.

Weak acid: HA uncharged below pKa; A− charged above pKa.

WhyThe uncharged HA equalises, so set it to 1 on each side. Gut: 1 + 10⁻² = 1.01. Blood: 1 + 10¹ = 11. Blood share = 11/12.01 ≈ 92%. A weak acid is trapped on the more basic side; 8% is the gut share.
Key factMethod: uncharged form = 1 in every compartment; total there = 1 + 10^(pH − pKa) for a weak acid (1 + 10^(pKa − pH) for a weak base); then take each share of the sum.
A weak acid accumulates on the more alkaline side (ion trapping); a weak base on the more acidic side.
Same pH on both sides → 50 : 50, whatever the pKa.

A patient begins breathing rapidly and exhales more CO2 than normal. Using CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−, what happens to blood pH?
  1. A. pH falls because H+ rises
  2. B. pH rises because H+ falls
  3. C. pH is unchanged because the kidneys compensate at once
  4. D. pH falls because HCO3− rises
  5. E. pH falls because carbonic acid accumulates
AnswerB. pH rises because H+ falls
WhyBlowing off CO2 pulls the reaction to the left, using up H+, so pH rises (respiratory alkalosis). Retaining CO2 pushes it right, making more H+, so pH falls. Kidneys need days, not seconds.
Key factCO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− (carbonic anhydrase).
↑PCO2 → ↑H+ → ↓pH; ↓PCO2 → ↓H+ → ↑pH.
So in acidemia, lowering PCO2 (hyperventilation) raises pH.

Not the kidney: ventilation of CO2 (lungs); "secretion of HCO3− into blood" (it is reabsorbed).

AnswerD. Chronic renal failure
WhyMetabolic acidosis normally makes healthy kidneys raise NH4+ excretion (as in DKA). Decreased NH4+ during acidosis means the kidneys cannot do it: renal failure. Emphysema and hyperventilation are respiratory, and vomiting causes alkalosis.
Key factMetabolic acidosis with working kidneys (e.g. DKA) → ↑NH4+ excretion (the highest of the usual options).

Chronic respiratory acidosis (emphysema) → ↑H+ excretion with a high HCO3−.

Arterial pH is 7.22 and PCO2 is 20 mm Hg. What is the plasma HCO3− (mEq/L)?
  1. A. 7.9
  2. B. 6.9
  3. C. 10
  4. D. 13.2
  5. E. 20
AnswerA. 7.9
WhypH = 6.1 + log(HCO3− / (0.03 × PCO2)). 7.22 − 6.1 = 1.12, so the ratio is 10^1.12 ≈ 13.2; multiply by 0.03 × 20 = 0.6 → 7.9 mEq/L. 13.2 is the ratio before multiplying.
Key factpH = 6.1 + log [HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2)
0.03 converts PCO2 in mm Hg to dissolved CO2 in mM; don't apply it to a CO2 already given in mEq/L.
Normal: 24 / (0.03 × 40 = 1.2) = 20; log 20 = 1.3 → pH 7.4.
Use 6.1 (Lecture 23), not 6.4 from the primer table.
q173 is keyed 8.7 by applying 0.03 to a CO2 already given as 20 mEq/L. By the lecture the factor converts only PCO2 in mm Hg: the answer is pKa + log(30/20) ≈ 7.18 with the slide's pKa 7 (6.28 with 6.1).

ABG: pH 7.33, PCO2 55 mm Hg, HCO3− 25 mEq/L. What is the primary disorder?
  1. A. No disorder; the values are near normal
  2. B. Metabolic acidosis
  3. C. Metabolic alkalosis
  4. D. Respiratory alkalosis
  5. E. Respiratory acidosis
AnswerE. Respiratory acidosis
WhyStep 1: pH below 7.40 → acidosis. Step 2: which value explains it? PCO2 above 40 explains the acidemia, while HCO3− 25 is normal (a metabolic acidosis needs a low HCO3−). So this is respiratory acidosis.
Key factReference points: pH 7.40 (7.35–7.45), PCO2 40 (33–44), HCO3− 24 (22–28).
1) pH below 7.40 = acidosis; above = alkalosis.
2) The value that explains the pH is primary:
  • ↓pH + ↓HCO3− = metabolic acidosis
  • ↓pH + ↑PCO2 = respiratory acidosis
  • ↑pH + ↑HCO3− = metabolic alkalosis
  • ↑pH + ↓PCO2 = respiratory alkalosis
The other value, if it moves the opposite way to the pH, is compensation.
q932 (pH 8.1, HCO3 35, PCO2 24) is keyed "metabolic alkalosis with compensation". The low PCO2 is not compensation (that would raise PCO2), so the gas is really a mixed metabolic and respiratory alkalosis. Pick the only metabolic-alkalosis option.

Which patient is most likely to have a primary respiratory acidosis?
  1. A. A patient on a ventilator set to too high a rate

WhyRespiratory acidosis = hypoventilation, so CO2 is retained. Opioids depress the respiratory center. Panic, altitude (hypoxemia), pulmonary embolism and an over-set ventilator all hyperventilate and cause respiratory alkalosis.
Key factRespiratory acidosis = ↓ alveolar ventilation → ↑PCO2 (pH below 7.40):
  • chronic lung disease: COPD, emphysema, chronic bronchitis (somnolence = CO2 narcosis); severe asthma (FEV1 under 40%)

  • nerve and muscle: myasthenia gravis, MS, Guillain–Barré; obesity hypoventilation
  • rarely ↑CO2 production (malignant hyperthermia)
Hypoventilation gives ↑PCO2 and ↓PO2.

  5. E. 7.50 / 47 / 35
AnswerE. 7.50 / 47 / 35
WhyVomiting loses gastric HCl → ↑HCO3−, ↑pH = metabolic alkalosis, kept going by volume contraction; hypoventilation raises PCO2 as compensation. D is a respiratory alkalosis (low PCO2).
Key factVomiting, bulimia, pyloric obstruction → loss of HCl → metabolic alkalosis.
Gas: ↑pH, ↑HCO3−, ↑PCO2 (compensatory hypoventilation, not above 55).
Clues: low Cl−, low K+, volume depletion (orthostasis), enamel erosion and parotid swelling.
Vomiting is a primary alkalosis, never a compensation.

Which pairing of cause and acid–base disorder is correct?
  1. A. Kidney failure — respiratory acidosis
  2. B. Acetazolamide — metabolic alkalosis
  3. C. Loop or thiazide diuretic — metabolic alkalosis
  4. D. Diarrhea — metabolic alkalosis
  5. E. Hyperaldosteronism — metabolic acidosis
AnswerC. Loop or thiazide diuretic — metabolic alkalosis
WhyLoop and thiazide diuretics (volume contraction, ↑aldosterone, H+ and K+ loss) cause metabolic alkalosis, as do hyperaldosteronism and antacids. Acetazolamide blocks HCO3− reabsorption → metabolic acidosis; diarrhea and kidney failure also cause metabolic acidosis.
Key factLecture table:
  • Respiratory acidosis — chronic lung disease
  • Respiratory alkalosis — hyperventilation; drug toxicity (analeptics, salicylates)
  • Metabolic acidosis — ↑ketogenesis (DKA), diarrhea, kidney failure; also salicylate, ethylene glycol, acetazolamide
  • Metabolic alkalosis — vomiting, salts of metabolic acids (lactate, ketoanions), NaHCO3 or antacids, loop and thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalemia
TA31 keys "Metabolic acidosis — DKA", but the COPD and panic-attack pairings in that question are also correct; only "metabolic alkalosis — severe diarrhea" is wrong. Drug-induced toxicity is matched to respiratory alkalosis (salicylates); opioids would cause respiratory acidosis.

A 30-year-old has had profuse watery diarrhea for 4 days. Blood pressure is low and skin turgor is poor. Arterial blood: pH 7.29, PCO2 29 mm Hg, HCO3− 14 mEq/L; serum K+ 2.8 mEq/L; anion gap normal. Which best explains the low serum K+?
  1. A. Buffering of the excess H+ by HCO3− consumes K+
  2. B. Volume depletion raises aldosterone, which drives renal K+ secretion (on top of K+ lost in stool)
  3. C. Decreased ADH lets K+ escape in a dilute urine
  4. D. Acidosis drives K+ into cells in exchange for H+ leaving them
  5. E. Hypoventilation retains CO2, which carries K+ into red cells
AnswerB. Volume depletion raises aldosterone, which drives renal K+ secretion (on top of K+ lost in stool)
WhyDiarrhea loses HCO3− and K+ in stool, and the volume loss raises aldosterone, which makes the distal tubule reabsorb Na+ and secrete K+ and H+. The tempting shift answer (D) runs the wrong way: in acidosis H+ moves into cells and K+ moves out, which would raise serum K+.
Key factK+ and H+ trade places across cell membranes, and aldosterone wastes both
  • Acidosis: H+ enters cells, K+ leaves → serum K+ ↑ (DKA can show normal or high K+ despite total-body loss)
  • Alkalosis: intracellular H+ is exchanged for extracellular K+ (H+ out, K+ in) → serum K+ ↓
  • Volume depletion (diarrhea, vomiting, diuretics) → renin–angiotensin → ↑aldosterone → distal tubule reabsorbs Na+, secretes K+ and H+ → hypokalemia (and in vomiting it keeps the alkalosis going)
  • Lecture cases: diarrhea → normal-gap acidosis with K+ 2.9; bulimia (vomiting) → metabolic alkalosis with K+ 2.6
The mechanism is renal physiology; the biochemistry lecture shows the low K+ in its diarrhea and bulimia cases without explaining it.

A patient with ethylene glycol poisoning has a high-AG metabolic acidosis. What is the body's first compensation?
  1. A. Breathing slows
  2. B. PCO2 rises
  3. C. The kidneys increase HCO3−
  4. D. PCO2 falls through hyperventilation
  5. E. HCO3− decreases further
AnswerD. PCO2 falls through hyperventilation
WhyCompensation uses the other system: metabolic problems → lungs (fast, minutes); respiratory problems → kidneys (slow, days). Low pH stimulates chemoreceptors → hyperventilation, ↓PCO2 (Kussmaul breathing). Renal HCO3− regeneration is real but slow.
Key fact
  • Metabolic acidosis → hyperventilation, ↓PCO2 (the lecture calls it compensatory respiratory alkalosis); the extra carbonic acid leaves as CO2 through the lungs
  • Metabolic alkalosis → hypoventilation, ↑PCO2
  • Respiratory acidosis → kidneys retain and make HCO3− (↑PCO2 → more H+ secreted → more HCO3− reabsorbed)
  • Respiratory alkalosis → kidneys excrete HCO3−
Lungs act in minutes; kidneys over days. Vomiting and diarrhea are never compensation.
q916 and q918 key "respiratory alkalosis" as the compensation for a diarrheal metabolic acidosis. That follows the lecture's wording ("compensated by respiratory alkalosis"); it means hyperventilation, not a second primary disorder.

A patient's pH is exactly 7.40, yet the anion gap is 20 mEq/L. What explains the normal pH?
  1. A. A second, opposing primary process (for example a metabolic alkalosis) is present

WhyCompensation never returns pH all the way to 7.40 while the cause persists. A normal pH alongside a clear abnormality means two primary disorders are cancelling (a mixed disorder). Full compensation (E) is the main trap.
Key factCompensation is partial: pH moves toward 7.4 but does not reach it while the cause continues.
pH 7.40 with an abnormal AG, HCO3− or PCO2 → a second primary process (mixed disorder).

Why does adding lactic acid raise the anion gap, while losing HCO3− in stool does not?
  1. A. Diarrhea adds unmeasured cations to plasma
  2. B. Diarrhea is a respiratory disorder
  3. C. Lactic acid raises the plasma Na+
  4. D. Lactic acid raises the plasma Cl−
  5. E. Lactate is an unmeasured anion that replaces the HCO3− it uses up; stool HCO3− loss is replaced by Cl−
AnswerE. Lactate is an unmeasured anion that replaces the HCO3− it uses up; stool HCO3− loss is replaced by Cl−
WhyAn added acid's H+ uses up HCO3−, and its anion (lactate, ketoacids, salicylate, formate, glycolate) is unmeasured, so the gap rises with a normal Cl− (normochloremic). Lost HCO3− is replaced by Cl− (hyperchloremic), so the gap stays normal.
Key factThe AG is used to sort metabolic acidosis:
  • Gain of acid → unmeasured anion accumulates → high AG, normochloremic
  • Loss of base (HCO3−) → replaced by Cl− → normal AG, hyperchloremic
A high AG means a metabolic acidosis is present, even when pH is normal.
AG = unmeasured anions − unmeasured cations.
TA33 and TA34 have no key marked in the TA file; by the lecture the answers are C (decreased HCO3− reflects either chloride replacement or unmeasured anions) and B (patient 1 accumulated chloride, patient 2 unmeasured anions).

RTA, diarrhea and acetazolamide are normal-gap.

A 55-year-old taking escalating aspirin doses for joint pain has tinnitus and a respiratory rate of 25. Which acid–base picture is classic?
  1. A. Respiratory acidosis plus metabolic alkalosis
  2. B. Early respiratory alkalosis, then high-AG metabolic acidosis
  3. C. Normal-AG metabolic acidosis
  4. D. Metabolic alkalosis with hypoventilation
  5. E. Respiratory acidosis only
AnswerB. Early respiratory alkalosis, then high-AG metabolic acidosis
WhySalicylate stimulates the respiratory center first (respiratory alkalosis, ↓PCO2), then uncouples oxidative phosphorylation → lactate and ketoacids plus the salicylate anion → high-AG metabolic acidosis. A PCO2 far below the expected compensation is the clue that both are present.
Key factAspirin (salicylate) overdose:
  • First: respiratory alkalosis (direct stimulation of the respiratory center)
  • Then: high-AG metabolic acidosis (salicylate, lactate, ketoacids)
  • Clues: tinnitus, tachypnea, a suicidal or confused patient with a high gap; PCO2 lower than expected
  • Treat: activated charcoal plus IV NaHCO3 to alkalinize the urine

Toxic and hypoxic acidoses

A patient in cardiogenic shock after a myocardial infarction is hypotensive with cool extremities. Which best explains the expected acid–base change?
  1. A. Chloride gain → normal-AG acidosis
  2. B. Loss of ketones in urine → metabolic alkalosis
  3. C. CO2 retention → respiratory acidosis only
  4. D. Lactate from anaerobic glycolysis → high-AG metabolic acidosis
  5. E. HCO3− retention by the kidneys → metabolic alkalosis
AnswerD. Lactate from anaerobic glycolysis → high-AG metabolic acidosis
WhyPoor perfusion = tissue hypoxia → pyruvate is reduced to lactate (LDH regenerates NAD+) → high-AG metabolic acidosis, tracked by serum lactate; hyperventilation compensates. The same logic covers CO poisoning, sickle crisis and heavy drinking.
Key factLactic acidosis = high-AG metabolic acidosis (↑lactate, ↓pH):
  • Tissue hypoxia: shock, MI, CO poisoning (blocks O2 delivery and cytochrome c oxidase; pulse oximetry falsely about 99%), sickle crisis
  • Alcohol: ↑NADH/NAD+ → pyruvate → lactate, plus ketone bodies
  • PDH deficiency (Farrah, Hosni): high lactate, pyruvate and alanine with normal glucose → lactic acidosis, not ketoacidosis
Tachypnea = compensatory hyperventilation (not CO2 retention). Measure serum lactate.

Mouth and stomach: the acid lipases

84unlocks 4TA ×2
A 4-week-old exclusively breastfed infant digests much of the fat in milk even though pancreatic lipase output is still low. Which feature describes the enzymes responsible?
  1. A. They are acid stable (pH 4–6) and prefer TAG with short- and medium-chain fatty acids
  2. B. They need bile salts to become active in the stomach
  3. C. They cut the C2 ester of phospholipids to give lysophospholipids
  4. D. They need colipase and work mainly in the duodenum
  5. E. They are secreted as zymogens and activated by trypsin
AnswerA. They are acid stable (pH 4–6) and prefer TAG with short- and medium-chain fatty acids
WhyLingual and gastric lipases are acid stable (pH 4–6), start TAG digestion in the mouth and stomach, and prefer short- and medium-chain TAG (milk, butter, coconut oil); they matter most in newborns and in pancreatic insufficiency such as cystic fibrosis. Colipase, bile salts and trypsin activation belong to the pancreatic phase in the duodenum, and cutting C2 is phospholipase A2.
Key factLingual (mouth) + gastric (stomach) lipase = the acid lipases
  • Start TAG digestion: TAG is the only dietary lipid whose digestion begins in the mouth (then stomach, then duodenum)
  • Acid stable, optimum pH 4–6; no colipase, no bile salts, not zymogens
  • Prefer TAG with short- and medium-chain FA (under 12 C): milk fat, butter, coconut oil
  • Significant in newborns (milk fat) and pancreatic insufficiency / cystic fibrosis → a patient with no pancreatic lipase can still digest short-chain (dairy) TAG

Pancreatic enzymes: lipase, colipase, PLA2, esterase

85unlocks 11
Which statement about pancreatic lipase is correct?
  1. A. It removes all three fatty acids, so TAG is absorbed as glycerol plus fatty acids
  2. B. It is secreted as a zymogen and activated in the jejunum
  3. C. It cleaves the C1 and C3 esters of long-chain TAG in the duodenum, leaving 2-monoacylglycerol
  4. D. It is inactivated by the bicarbonate released in response to secretin
  5. E. It accounts for less TAG digestion than lingual lipase
AnswerC. It cleaves the C1 and C3 esters of long-chain TAG in the duodenum, leaving 2-monoacylglycerol
WhyPancreatic lipase is the main TAG-digesting enzyme; in the duodenum it cuts the C1 and C3 esters of long-chain TAG, giving 2-MAG + 2 free FA, the form that enters enterocytes. It is secreted active and works at the neutral pH that bicarbonate creates; it is acid (as in Zollinger-Ellison) that inactivates it.
Key factPancreatic lipase = the main TAG enzyme, acting in the duodenum
  • Most lipid digestion: duodenum + pancreatic lipase (the acid lipases add only a little)
  • Cuts esters at C1 and C3 of long-chain TAG → 2-monoacylglycerol + 2 FFA (an isomerase lets a little go on to glycerol)
  • Lipid crosses the brush border as 2-MAG + FFA: not intact TAG, not DAG, not mostly glycerol
  • Secreted active (not a zymogen) into the duodenum; needs colipase. CF: it never reaches the gut → long-chain TAG undigested
  • Destroyed by acid: gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) floods the duodenum with HCl → lipase inactivated → steatorrhea

Pancreatic juice contains an enzyme, activated by trypsin, that acts on dietary phosphatidylcholine in the small intestine. Which products does it release?
  1. A. Phosphatidic acid and choline

AnswerC. A lysophospholipid and the fatty acid from carbon 2
WhyPhospholipase A2 (secreted as pro-PLA2, activated by trypsin) cleaves the ester at C2, releasing the R2 fatty acid and leaving a lysophospholipid. DAG + phosphocholine is phospholipase C, phosphatidic acid + choline is phospholipase D, and free cholesterol + FA is cholesterol esterase.

  • Phospholipase A2: cuts the ester at C2 (R2) → lysophospholipid + FA; secreted as pro-PLA2, activated by trypsin
  • Cholesterol esterase: cholesteryl ester = FA on the C3-OH of cholesterol → hydrolyzed to free cholesterol + FA
  • Where each class is digested: TAG mouth → stomach → duodenum; phospholipid and cholesteryl ester only in the duodenum (pancreatic enzymes)

  1. A. I cells; fatty acids and peptides in the duodenum

Bile: composition, emulsification, bile acids

89unlocks 7TA ×1
Bile is collected from the gallbladder of a healthy volunteer. According to the lecture, which statement about it is correct?
  1. A. It contains free fatty acids secreted by hepatocytes
  2. B. It is made by the gallbladder and released in response to secretin
  3. C. Its main lipid is free cholesterol, about 85%
  4. D. Its bile salts are made from bilirubin
  5. E. Bile salts are its main lipid (about 85%), and bile salts plus phospholipid keep its cholesterol dissolved
AnswerE. Bile salts are its main lipid (about 85%), and bile salts plus phospholipid keep its cholesterol dissolved
WhyBile is made by hepatocytes, then stored and concentrated 10–20x in the gallbladder; its lipids are about 85% bile salts, 10% free cholesterol, 5% phospholipid (lecture numbers), and bile salts + phospholipid solubilize cholesterol, preventing stones. Bile has no fatty acids, it is released on CCK, and bile salts come from cholesterol (bilirubin, from heme, is the pigment).
Key factBile: where it is made, what it contains, what it does
  • Made by hepatocytes; stored and concentrated 10–20x in the gallbladder; released on CCK
  • Lipids: 85% bile salts, 10% free cholesterol, 5% phospholipid (lecture); also water, electrolytes, bilirubin; no fatty acids
  • Bile acids are made from cholesterol in the liver (rate-limiting enzyme 7α-hydroxylase)
  • Four functions: (1) main route to excrete excess cholesterol; (2) bile acids + phospholipids keep cholesterol in solution (no stones); (3) emulsify TAG for pancreatic lipase; (4) help absorb fat-soluble vitamins
  • The bile component that matters for fat digestion and absorption is the bile salts (not cholesterol, lecithin or bilirubin)
q979 and lecture slide 18 give 85% bile salts, 10% cholesterol, 5% phospholipid; most physiology texts give phospholipid a larger share than cholesterol. Answer with the course numbers.
