Bile: composition, emulsification, bile acids

90unlocks 6TA ×2
A patient with cirrhosis makes very little bile and has steatorrhea, although their pancreatic enzyme output is normal. What does bile normally do for fat digestion?
  1. A. Activates pancreatic lipase from its zymogen
  2. B. Carries intact micelles across the enterocyte membrane
  3. C. Converts dietary lipids into cholesterol
  4. D. Emulsifies fat into small droplets, increasing the surface area for pancreatic lipase
  5. E. Hydrolyzes TAG into monoglycerides and fatty acids
AnswerD. Emulsifies fat into small droplets, increasing the surface area for pancreatic lipase
WhyBile salts are amphipathic detergents; with peristalsis they emulsify fat in the duodenum into small, stable droplets that do not coalesce, giving water-soluble lipase more surface area. They never hydrolyze TAG, and lipase is not a zymogen. Less bile → less emulsification → maldigestion.
Key factBile salts emulsify; they do not digest
  • Emulsification happens in the duodenum (not mouth, stomach or colon) by bile salts (detergent) + peristalsis (mixing)
  • Result: smaller, stable droplets kept from coalescing → ↑ surface area for pancreatic lipase
  • Bile salts do not hydrolyze TAG, activate lipase or enter the enterocyte; after digestion they form mixed micelles
  • Liver disease / bile obstruction → ↓ emulsification → fat less accessible to lipase → steatorrhea (course: maldigestion)

91unlocks 10TA ×1
Researchers compare cholic acid with glycocholate. Why is the glycine-conjugated form the better emulsifier in the duodenum?
  1. A. Conjugation lets it hydrolyze TAG ester bonds
  2. B. Conjugation raises its pKa, so it stays protonated
  3. C. Conjugation happens in the gut and lets it diffuse across the enterocyte membrane
  4. D. Conjugation lowers its pKa, so it stays ionized and more amphipathic at intestinal pH
  5. E. Conjugation makes it more hydrophobic, so it dissolves inside the fat droplet
AnswerD. Conjugation lowers its pKa, so it stays ionized and more amphipathic at intestinal pH
WhyIn the liver, bile acids are joined by an amide bond to glycine or taurine. This lowers the pKa (to about 2–4), so at intestinal pH they are ionized Na+/K+ bile salts, more amphipathic and better detergents. Lower pKa means a better emulsifier, and ionized salts do not diffuse across membranes.
Key factConjugation: glycine/taurine → lower pKa → bile salt → better detergent
  • Done in the liver; amide bond with glycine or taurine only (not cholesterol, not other amino acids)
  • Lowers pKa (about 2–4) → ionized at intestinal pH → bile salt (Na+/K+ salt) = the ionized, conjugated form of a bile acid
  • More amphipathic and water soluble → more effective emulsifier: lower pKa = better
  • Ionized bile salts do not cross membranes passively (the ileum uses a Na+ cotransporter); secreted bile acids are conjugated
  • Cannot conjugate → poor emulsification and micelles → steatorrhea

A stool sample is analyzed for bile acids. Which one is formed by bacterial action and found mainly in feces?

  2. B. Lithocholic acid

  5. E. Chenodeoxycholic acid

WhyGut bacteria deconjugate and 7α-dehydroxylate the primary bile acids: cholic → deoxycholic, chenodeoxycholic → lithocholic; these secondary, unconjugated acids make up most of the fecal loss. Key factPrimary vs secondary bile acids
  • Primary (made in the liver from cholesterol): cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid (conjugated forms: glycocholic, taurocholic, etc.)
  • Secondary (made by intestinal bacteria: deconjugation + 7α-dehydroxylation): deoxycholic (from cholic) and lithocholic (from chenodeoxycholic)
  • Fecal bile acids = mostly secondary (deoxycholic, lithocholic), deconjugated
  • Deconjugation is done by intestinal flora, not brush border enzymes or lipase

Enterohepatic circulation and bile acid drugs

93unlocks 9TA ×1
A 30-year-old with Crohn disease has their terminal ileum resected. Months later they have watery diarrhea and greasy stools. Which lost process explains both findings?
  1. A. Bile acid synthesis in the liver
  2. B. Gallbladder storage of bile
  3. C. Bile salt reabsorption, so bile acids spill into the colon and the bile salt pool shrinks
  4. D. Pancreatic lipase secretion
  5. E. Cholesterol uptake by NPC1L1
AnswerC. Bile salt reabsorption, so bile acids spill into the colon and the bile salt pool shrinks
WhyAbout 95–98% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum by a Na+ cotransporter and return to the liver in portal blood (enterohepatic circulation). Without the ileum, bile acids reach the colon (diarrhea, bile in stool) and the shrinking pool cannot make enough micelles (steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin loss); liver synthesis, gallbladder storage and pancreatic lipase are intact.
Key factEnterohepatic circulation
  • 95–98% of bile salts reabsorbed in the terminal (distal) ileum via Na+ cotransport → portal vein → liver; each molecule recycles about 10x/day
  • Only about 5% is lost in feces and replaced by new synthesis, so secreted bile is mostly recycled bile salt, not new
  • Ileal resection or Crohn ileitis → bile acids lost → ↑ bile in stool (diarrhea), ↓ pool → steatorrhea + ↓ A, D, E, K (and B12)
  • Bile's job is to solubilize and absorb lipids; it is reabsorbed in the terminal ileum (not duodenum or colon)
Lecture slide 23 says 98% recycling; practice keys say 95%. Either is accepted.

Enterohepatic circulation and bile acid drugs

94unlocks 12
A patient with an LDL of 190 mg/dL starts a positively charged resin that is not absorbed from the gut. What is its main mechanism, and which side effect should they be warned about?
  1. A. Binds bile acids and blocks their ileal reabsorption; vitamin K malabsorption
  2. B. Replaces dietary fat with a nondigestible sucrose polyester; gallstones
  3. C. Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase; myopathy
  4. D. Inhibits pancreatic lipase; oily stools
  5. E. Blocks NPC1L1 cholesterol uptake; vitamin B12 deficiency
AnswerA. Binds bile acids and blocks their ileal reabsorption; vitamin K malabsorption
WhyCholestyramine (and colesevelam) are anion-exchange resins that bind negatively charged bile acids and block the enterohepatic circulation; the liver diverts more cholesterol into bile acids, LDL receptors rise and serum LDL falls. Binding bile acids also impairs micelles, so fat-soluble vitamins (K) are lost. Lipase inhibition is orlistat; NPC1L1 blockade is ezetimibe.
Key factDrugs that act on fat digestion and absorption
  • Cholestyramine / colesevelam (bile acid sequestrant, positively charged resin): binds bile acids in the gut → blocks enterohepatic reabsorption → more cholesterol made into bile acids → ↑ LDL receptors → ↓ LDL. Side effect: ↓ fat-soluble vitamins (vitamin K); space other drugs
  • Orlistat: inhibits gastric + pancreatic lipase → TAG not hydrolyzed (about 1/3 of fat lost) → oily, foul steatorrhea
  • Ezetimibe: blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1)
  • Olestra: nondigestible fat substitute (sucrose + 6–8 FA). Ursodeoxycholic / chenodeoxycholic acid: dissolve cholesterol gallstones

Gallstones (cholelithiasis)

95unlocks 8TA ×3
A 44-year-old obese woman with three children has RUQ pain after fatty meals, and ultrasound shows cholesterol stones. Which change in bile directly causes them?
  1. A. Increased bilirubin from hemolysis
  2. B. Low calcium in bile
  3. C. Increased pancreatic lipase secretion
  4. D. More bile salt and phospholipid relative to cholesterol
  5. E. More cholesterol than bile salts and phospholipid can keep in solution
AnswerE. More cholesterol than bile salts and phospholipid can keep in solution
WhyCholesterol stones form when bile is supersaturated: either more cholesterol enters bile (obesity, estrogen, pregnancy, diabetes, fibrates) or there are fewer bile acids (low 7α-hydroxylase, ileal disease, biliary obstruction, liver failure). Excess bilirubin from hemolysis gives black pigment stones instead.
Key factCholelithiasis
  • Mechanism: more cholesterol enters bile than bile salts + phospholipid can solubilize → cholesterol precipitates (most common stone)
  • ↓ Bile acids: ileal disease (bile acid malabsorption), biliary obstruction, liver failure, ↓ 7α-hydroxylase (fibrates such as fenofibrate inhibit it)
  • ↑ Biliary cholesterol: obesity, estrogen/contraceptives, pregnancy, diabetes, fibrates. Decreased cholesterol excretion is never a cause
  • 5 Fs: fat, female, fertile, forty, fair (age 30 and below is not a risk)
  • Black pigment stones: chronic hemolysis (e.g., hereditary spherocytosis)
  • Clinic: RUQ pain after a fatty meal (CCK) radiating under the right shoulder; ultrasound; jaundice + clay stool = duct blocked; after cholecystectomy, limited tolerance for fatty food

Micelles and absorption

96unlocks 11TA ×1
A patient has a common bile duct stone, and no bile reaches the gut. Which dietary component will still be absorbed normally?
  1. A. Stearic acid (C18)
  2. B. Octanoic acid (C8)
  3. C. Retinol
  4. D. Cholesterol
  5. E. Vitamin K
AnswerB. Octanoic acid (C8)
WhyShort- and medium-chain FA (under 12 C, e.g., C8) enter enterocytes without mixed micelles and go straight to portal blood. Long-chain FA (C18), 2-MAG, cholesterol and vitamins A, D, E, K must ride in bile-salt micelles, so they fail when bile is absent.
Key factMixed micelles and what needs them
  • Structure: bile salts and other amphipathic lipids with hydrophilic groups outside, hydrophobic inside; core = 2-MAG, LCFA, cholesterol, lysophospholipid, vitamins A D E K
  • Job: the hydrophilic, water-soluble surface carries hydrophobic lipids through the watery lumen to the brush border (jejunum)
  • Micelles are not absorbed intact: their contents enter the enterocyte; bile salts stay in the lumen for the ileum
  • Need micelles: LCFA, 2-MAG, cholesterol, fat-soluble vitamins. Do not: short/medium-chain FA (under 12 C) → directly to portal blood, not lymph; glycerol, amino acids, B12 (intrinsic factor), bile acids (ileal transporter)
  • Sequence: micelles → FFA + 2-MAG enter the cell → chylomicrons → lymph
Lecture slide 14 has a garbled line ('short and medium chain fatty acid-lymphatic-portal circulation'); its meaning, and q1033/q1139, is that short/medium chains go to portal blood, not lymph.

A child with abetalipoproteinemia has fat-laden enterocytes, steatorrhea and almost no plasma chylomicrons. Which step is defective?

Key factRe-esterification and the chylomicron
  • Enterocyte ER: FA → acyl-CoA; 2-MAG + 2 acyl-CoA → TAG; cholesterol → CE (ACAT); lysophospholipid → PL. Purpose: re-make complex lipids for packaging and transport
  • MTP loads them onto apoB-48 → nascent chylomicron (needs protein synthesis). MTP loss = abetalipoproteinemia; chylomicron retention disease → fat + A D E K malabsorption
  • Chylomicron = made by the intestine, most TAG (85–90%), largest, lowest density, carries dietary (exogenous) TAG to muscle and adipose
  • Too big for capillaries → lacteal → lymph → thoracic duct → blood (chyle richest in intestinal lymph); plasma lipemic after a fatty meal; ↑ in fed state
  • Compare: VLDL = liver TAG; LDL = cholesterol to tissues; HDL = reverse cholesterol transport

Hours after a fatty meal, a patient's plasma stays milky. Their chylomicrons contain normal apoB-48, but fatty acids are not released from them in capillaries. Which apoprotein is most likely missing?

  4. D. Apo(a)

AnswerA. ApoC-II
WhyApoC-II, picked up from HDL, activates capillary lipoprotein lipase, which frees fatty acids from chylomicron and VLDL TAG; without it TAG-rich particles persist. ApoB-100 binds the LDL receptor, apoE mediates remnant uptake by the liver and apoA-I activates LCAT.
Key factApoprotein table
  • ApoB-48: made only in enterocytes (apoB mRNA editing → stop codon, 48% length, no LDL-receptor domain); unique to chylomicrons; required to assemble and secrete them
  • ApoB-100: full length, liver; VLDL/LDL; ligand for the LDL receptor
  • ApoC-II: from HDL; activates lipoprotein lipase → deficiency = hypertriglyceridemia (chylomicrons persist)
  • ApoE: from HDL; remnant uptake by hepatocytes. ApoA-I: HDL, activates LCAT
  • LPL (capillary wall): chylomicron TAG → FA to muscle/adipose, glycerol to liver; chylomicrons lose FA as they circulate and become remnants

A 3-year-old with recurrent pneumonia, a positive sweat chloride test and bulky, floating stools has a stool fat analysis. Which pattern is expected?
  1. A. Normal digestion; excess cholesterol in stool
  2. B. Maldigestion; mostly lactose and sucrose in stool
  3. C. Maldigestion; mostly undigested triglycerides in stool
  4. D. Malabsorption; mostly bile salts in stool
  5. E. Malabsorption; mostly free fatty acids in stool
AnswerC. Maldigestion; mostly undigested triglycerides in stool
WhyIn cystic fibrosis, thick secretions plug the pancreatic ducts, so lipase (and amylase and proteases) never reach the duodenum: maldigestion with TAG in stool. Mucosal disease (Crohn, celiac, infection) is malabsorption with fatty acids in stool. Brush-border disaccharidases are intact in CF, so lactose and sucrose are still digested.
Key factSteatorrhea = frothy, foul-smelling, floating stool with excess fat
  • Maldigestion → TAG in stool: pancreatic insufficiency (cystic fibrosis, chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer), Zollinger-Ellison (acid kills lipase), liver disease / ↓ bile (↓ emulsification)
  • Malabsorption → fatty acids in stool: intestinal disease (Crohn, celiac, bacterial or parasitic disease)
  • CF: lung infections + steatorrhea + failure to thrive + ↑ sweat Cl- (or meconium ileus) → pancreatic ducts plugged → no pancreatic lipase, amylase or proteases (starch, TAG, protein undigested; lactose/sucrose fine); treat with oral enzymes
  • Chronic pancreatitis → steatorrhea + diabetes
  • Not causes: obesity, ↑ CCK, kidney stones

  • A (retinol, β-carotene): night blindness, blurry vision

  • E: hemolysis, neuropathy
  • K: easy bruising, bleeding, ↑ PT / clotting time (no γ-carboxylation of Glu on factors II, VII, IX, X)
  • Causes seen: CF, pancreatitis, gallstone/bile obstruction, cholecystitis, celiac, Crohn/ileal loss, chylomicron retention, bile acid sequestrants

The fed state and insulin

101unlocks 9TA ×1
Two hours after a large pasta dinner, which set of changes is expected in a person's hepatocytes?
  1. A. Glucagon is high, PEPCK is induced and ketogenesis increases
  2. B. Hormone-sensitive lipase is phosphorylated and fatty acid oxidation increases
  3. C. Insulin-activated protein phosphatase dephosphorylates glycogen synthase, pyruvate kinase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, all of which are active
  4. D. The low-insulin state drives fatty acid synthesis in the mitochondrial matrix
  5. E. Glycogen phosphorylase is phosphorylated and active, and CPT-I activity rises
AnswerC. Insulin-activated protein phosphatase dephosphorylates glycogen synthase, pyruvate kinase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, all of which are active
WhyAfter a meal the insulin/glucagon ratio is high; insulin activates protein phosphatase, so the storage enzymes (glycogen synthase, pyruvate kinase, PFK-2, ACC) sit in their active dephosphorylated form. Phosphorylase, CPT-I, PEPCK, HSL and ketogenesis are fasting events, and fatty acid synthesis is cytosolic and needs high insulin.
Key factFatty acid synthesis = well-fed, high-insulin, high-ATP state.
  • Where: cytosol; mainly liver and lactating mammary gland, less so adipose.
  • Insulin → protein phosphatase → dephosphorylated = active storage enzymes: glycogen synthase, pyruvate kinase, PFK-2, acetyl-CoA carboxylase. Insulin is the hormone that promotes lipogenesis.
  • The fed state switches OFF: lipolysis (HSL), β-oxidation (CPT-I), ketogenesis, gluconeogenesis (pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase), glycogenolysis, muscle proteolysis.
  • A low-insulin state never promotes fatty acid synthesis (true or false: false).
  • Lecture summary table: rate-limiting enzyme ACC; needs ATP; activator citrate; inhibitor long-chain acyl-CoA; clinical link alcoholic fatty liver.
q1168 keys pyruvate carboxylase as inhibited after a meal; it is not directly insulin-regulated, so it is reached by eliminating the four insulin-activated enzymes. The TA67 answer table lists ATP/ADP under inhibitors; the lecture names long-chain acyl-CoA (palmitoyl-CoA) as the ACC inhibitor.

A 30-year-old man drinks two liters of fructose-sweetened soda daily and develops hypertriglyceridemia. Why does a fructose load drive hepatic fat synthesis more readily than glucose?
  1. A. Fructose enters glycolysis below PFK-1 as DHAP and glyceraldehyde, bypassing its regulation
  2. B. Fructose inhibits fatty acid synthase, diverting acetyl-CoA into TAG
  3. C. Fructose raises glucagon, which dephosphorylates and activates PFK-2
  4. D. Fructose is phosphorylated by hexokinase in adipose tissue and enters glycolysis at PFK-1
  5. E. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate inhibits PFK-1 after a fructose load
AnswerA. Fructose enters glycolysis below PFK-1 as DHAP and glyceraldehyde, bypassing its regulation
WhyFructokinase and aldolase B split fructose-1-phosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde, which enter glycolysis below PFK-1, so hepatic flux is fast and unregulated and supplies glycerol 3-phosphate and acetyl-CoA for TAG. Glucose must pass PFK-1, which insulin opens through fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; F-2,6-BP activates PFK-1, it never inhibits it.
Key factPFK-1 is the glycolysis gate in the fed liver.
  • Insulin → dephosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme → PFK-2 active → ↑ fructose-2,6-bisphosphate → ↑ PFK-1, ↓ fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase → glycolysis → acetyl-CoA for lipogenesis.
  • Glucagon or hypoglycemia: PKA phosphorylates the enzyme → FBPase-2 active → less F-2,6-BP → gluconeogenesis favored.
  • Fructose bypasses PFK-1: fructokinase → fructose-1-P → aldolase B → DHAP + glyceraldehyde (glyceraldehyde → glycerol → hepatic glycerol kinase → glycerol 3-P). Mainly hepatic, fast, unregulated → readily makes triglycerides.
What it unlocks: 7 questions

Phase I: acetyl-CoA out as citrate, plus NADPH

104unlocks 9TA ×2
Which statement correctly pairs the phases of fatty acid synthesis with their enzymes?
  1. A. Phase I: carboxylation of 3C acetyl-CoA to 2C malonyl-CoA; Phase II: citrate export; Phase III: fatty acid synthase
  2. B. Phase I: ATP-citrate lyase makes cytosolic acetyl-CoA; Phase II: ACC makes malonyl-CoA; Phase III: fatty acid synthase builds palmitate
  3. C. Phase I: ACC makes malonyl-CoA in mitochondria and exports it; Phase II: ATP-citrate lyase; Phase III: thioesterase II
  4. D. Phase I: fatty acid synthase; Phase II: elongase; Phase III: desaturase
  5. E. Phase I: cytosolic pyruvate dehydrogenase; Phase II: malic enzyme; Phase III: ACC
AnswerB. Phase I: ATP-citrate lyase makes cytosolic acetyl-CoA; Phase II: ACC makes malonyl-CoA; Phase III: fatty acid synthase builds palmitate
WhyThe course scheme is I citrate out and cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase, II ACC carboxylates 2C acetyl-CoA to 3C malonyl-CoA, III FAS adds 2C units and thioesterase releases palmitate. Malonyl-CoA is never made in mitochondria, and the reversed carbon counts (3C acetyl, 2C malonyl) are a planted trap.
Key factThree phases
  • I Production of cytosolic acetyl-CoA: citrate exported, cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase.
  • II Carboxylation: ACC, 2C acetyl-CoA → 3C malonyl-CoA (committed, rate-limiting).
  • III Chain building on fatty acid synthase → palmitate (16:0), released by thioesterase.
Regulated at three enzymes: ATP-citrate lyase (induced by glucose/insulin), ACC (allosteric, covalent, gene expression), FAS (gene expression: insulin, feeding ↑; PUFA, fasting ↓). Not regulators: thioesterase, NADPH (a substrate). Blocking ATP-citrate lyase → less cytosolic acetyl-CoA for ACC.

  • TA: put the whole sequence in order; drug blocks ATP-citrate lyase → less cytosolic acetyl-CoA for carboxylation.

In a well-fed hepatocyte, high ATP and NADH slow the TCA cycle. Which step is inhibited, and how does that feed fatty acid synthesis?
  1. A. Citrate synthase is inhibited, so acetyl-CoA diffuses directly into the cytosol
  2. B. Pyruvate dehydrogenase is inhibited, so pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA in the cytosol
  3. C. ATP-citrate lyase is inhibited, so malonyl-CoA is exported from the mitochondria
  4. D. Isocitrate dehydrogenase is inhibited, so citrate builds up, is exported, and is cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase into acetyl-CoA plus oxaloacetate

AnswerD. Isocitrate dehydrogenase is inhibited, so citrate builds up, is exported, and is cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase into acetyl-CoA plus oxaloacetate
WhyAcetyl-CoA made by PDH cannot cross the inner membrane. High ATP/NADH inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase, citrate accumulates and leaves on the citrate translocase, and cytosolic ATP-citrate lyase regenerates acetyl-CoA (and OAA). Acetylcarnitine is the β-oxidation carrier going the other way.
Key fact
  • Carbons for fat come from dietary carbohydrate: glucose → pyruvate → (PDH, mitochondria) acetyl-CoA.
  • Acetyl-CoA cannot cross the inner membrane → with OAA (citrate synthase) → citrate → exits on the citrate translocase (tricarboxylate carrier).
  • High ATP and NADH inhibit isocitrate dehydrogenase → citrate accumulates → exported.
  • Cytosol: ATP-citrate lyase (spends ATP) → acetyl-CoA + OAA. Acetyl-CoA is the immediate carbon source; cytosolic citrate also activates ACC. OAA → malate → pyruvate (malic enzyme, NADPH).
  • Never the exported form: acetyl-CoA itself, malonyl-CoA, acetylcarnitine, malate, pyruvate.

A mouse lacking cytosolic malic enzyme has reduced hepatic fatty acid synthesis. Which reaction normally supplies the missing cofactor, and where is it used?
  1. A. Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA; NADPH for ATP-citrate lyase
  2. B. Malate → pyruvate + CO2; NADPH for the two reduction steps on fatty acid synthase
  3. C. Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (NAD+-linked); NADH for fatty acid synthase
  4. D. Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; NADPH for thioesterase
  5. E. Oxaloacetate → malate; NADH for acetyl-CoA carboxylase
AnswerB. Malate → pyruvate + CO2; NADPH for the two reduction steps on fatty acid synthase
WhyMalic enzyme oxidatively decarboxylates malate to pyruvate + CO2 and reduces NADP+ to NADPH, which FAS uses for its two reductions per cycle. ACC needs no NADPH, and glycolysis, PDH and NAD+-isocitrate dehydrogenase make NADH, not NADPH.
Key factNADPH sources
  • Pentose phosphate pathway (HMP shunt; oxidative phase: G6PD, 6-phosphogluconate DH; glucose 6-P → ribulose 5-P) = the chief source.
  • Malic enzyme: malate → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH (about half the NADPH for FA synthesis); its malate comes from the OAA released by ATP-citrate lyase (OAA → malate by malate DH, using NADH).
  • Used by FAS's two reductases (14 per palmitate) and by cholesterol synthesis; ACC uses none.
  • NOT NADPH sources: glycolysis, TCA, ETC/oxidative phosphorylation, β-oxidation, gluconeogenesis, hexokinase, urea cycle. Glutathione reductase and FA synthesis consume NADPH.
  • G6PD deficiency or inhibition → less NADPH → less fatty acid synthesis.
q1201 keys the HMP shunt as the major NADPH source over malic enzyme; the lecture calls the pentose phosphate pathway the chief source and also says malic enzyme supplies about 50%, so take PPP only when 'major' is asked.

Which reaction is the committed and rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis, with its correct requirements?
  1. A. Acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase; needs NADPH, ATP and biotin
  2. B. Palmitoyl-ACP → palmitate by thioesterase; needs water
  3. C. Pyruvate → oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase; needs biotin and ATP
  4. D. Acetyl-CoA (2C) → malonyl-CoA (3C) by acetyl-CoA carboxylase; needs biotin, ATP and CO2
  5. E. Citrate → acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate by ATP-citrate lyase; needs ATP and CoA
AnswerD. Acetyl-CoA (2C) → malonyl-CoA (3C) by acetyl-CoA carboxylase; needs biotin, ATP and CO2
WhyAcetyl-CoA carboxylase carboxylates acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA using biotin, ATP and CO2 (HCO3−); this is the committed, rate-limiting step. NADPH belongs to fatty acid synthase, and pyruvate carboxylase also uses biotin but serves gluconeogenesis.
Key factAcetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) = committed and rate-limiting step.
  • Acetyl-CoA (2C) + HCO3−/CO2 + ATP → malonyl-CoA (3C) + ADP + Pi, in the cytosol.
  • Cofactors: biotin (B7), ATP, CO2. Two half-reactions: ATP carboxylates biotin, then biotin hands CO2 to acetyl-CoA.
  • No NADPH and no AMP (NADPH is used by FAS; AMP inhibits ACC through AMPK).
  • Not rate-limiting: ATP-citrate lyase, fatty acid synthase, malic enzyme, PDH, citrate synthase, malate DH, thioesterase, pyruvate or propionyl-CoA carboxylase.

A 26-year-old bodybuilder who eats a dozen raw egg whites daily develops periorificial dermatitis, alopecia and fasting hypoglycemia. Which pair of enzymes is impaired?
  1. A. PEPCK and fatty acid synthase
  2. B. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and ATP-citrate lyase
  3. C. Glucose-6-phosphatase and malic enzyme
  4. D. Pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
  5. E. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase and pyruvate carboxylase

WhyEgg-white avidin binds biotin (B7), the CO2 carrier of the carboxylases: acetyl-CoA carboxylase (no malonyl-CoA) and pyruvate carboxylase (first step of gluconeogenesis, hence fasting hypoglycemia). PDH and α-KG DH use thiamine, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses B12.
Key factBiotin = vitamin B7, covalently attached to a lysine (biotinylation) of three carboxylases:
  • Acetyl-CoA carboxylase: acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA (fatty acid synthesis).
  • Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate → OAA, first step of gluconeogenesis → deficiency gives fasting hypoglycemia.
  • Propionyl-CoA carboxylase: odd-chain catabolism.
Causes: raw egg-white avidin, bacterial streptavidin, biotinidase deficiency (cannot recycle biotin). Signs: periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, brittle nails, paresthesias. Not biotin: PDH (B1), transaminases (B6), methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12), CoA (B5).

A mutation makes acetyl-CoA carboxylase resistant to phosphorylation. During a 24-hour fast, what is expected in the liver?
  1. A. ACC stays active, and malonyl-CoA activates CPT-I, raising ketogenesis
  2. B. Malonyl-CoA activates hormone-sensitive lipase, increasing lipolysis

Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I; it never activates it.
Key factCovalent (short-term) control of ACC
  • Insulin → ↓cAMP, protein phosphatase → dephosphorylated ACC = active.
  • Glucagon, epinephrine (cAMP/PKA) and AMP → AMPK → phosphorylated ACC = inactive (exercise, fasting, low energy, insulin deficiency).
  • Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, so synthesis and β-oxidation never run together.
    ACC on → malonyl-CoA ↑ → CPT-I blocked → ↓ β-oxidation, ↓ ketones.
    ACC off → malonyl-CoA ↓ → CPT-I free → ↑ β-oxidation (marathon runner).
  • Inhibitors of fatty acid synthesis: glucagon, epinephrine, AMP. Activators: insulin, citrate.

Which statement about mammalian fatty acid synthase is correct?
  1. A. It builds the chain from the carboxyl (α) end toward the methyl (ω) end
  2. B. Its monomer is fully active, with the intermediates free in solution
  3. C. Each cycle is dehydration, oxidation, condensation, oxidation, using NAD+
  4. D. It is a filamentous polymer activated by citrate
  5. E. It is a dimer of identical multifunctional polypeptides, each with seven activities and an ACP; each cycle is condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction
AnswerE. It is a dimer of identical multifunctional polypeptides, each with seven activities and an ACP; each cycle is condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction
WhyFAS is a head-to-tail dimer of identical polypeptides, each with all seven activities plus an ACP; only the dimer works. Each turn is condensation → reduction → dehydration → reduction (both reductions use NADPH), and the first acetyl becomes the ω end, so the chain grows ω → α. The citrate-activated filament is ACC.
Key factFatty acid synthase (FAS)
  • Dimer of identical polypeptides, head to tail; each has all 7 activities + ACP (phosphopantetheine arm carries the chain). Only the dimer is active.
  • Each 2C cycle: condensation (−CO2) → reduction (NADPH) → dehydration → reduction (NADPH).
  • The primer acetyl becomes the methyl (ω) end; new 2C units go on at the carboxyl end → chain grows ω → α. The α end (C1) is the carboxyl group.

  • 1 acetyl-CoA primer + 7 malonyl-CoA = 8 acetyl-CoA in all; 7 cycles.

  • Directly required: acetyl-CoA, ATP, NADPH (plus biotin and CO2; citrate carries acetyl units and activates ACC; OAA makes citrate).
  • Not required: GTP, NADH, FADH2, propionyl-CoA, isocitrate, AMP, glycerol 3-phosphate.

WhyΔ6 desaturation gives 18:3(Δ6,9,12); elongation adds 2 carbons at the carboxyl end, so every Δ number rises by 2: 20:3(Δ8,11,14). Arachidonic acid (20:4) needs a further Δ5 desaturation, and the ω number never changes with elongation.
Key fact
  • Palmitate is first activated to palmitoyl-CoA.
  • Elongation by elongase in the smooth ER (2C donor malonyl-CoA) and in mitochondria (donor acetyl-CoA, 2 C); NADPH reduces.
  • Desaturases are in the ER. Δ9 (stearoyl-CoA) desaturase places the first double bond between C9 and C10 (stearate 18:0 → oleate 18:1Δ9). Humans have Δ9, Δ6, Δ5, Δ4 only.
  • Δ counts from the carboxyl carbon (C1); ω from the methyl end. Elongation → each Δ + 2, ω unchanged.

Triacylglycerol synthesis and storage

Which sequence describes hepatic triacylglycerol synthesis?
  1. A. Fatty acyl-CoA is converted to free fatty acids by acyl-CoA synthetase before GPAT acts
  2. B. Free fatty acids are joined directly to glycerol 3-P by lipoprotein lipase
  3. C. Fatty acids → fatty acyl-CoA; glycerol 3-P → lysophosphatidic acid (GPAT) → phosphatidic acid (AGPAT) → DAG (phosphatidic acid phosphatase) → TAG (DGAT)
  4. D. Glycerol 3-P → DAG (DGAT) → phosphatidic acid (AGPAT) → TAG (GPAT)
  5. E. Free glycerol is acylated by MGAT in adipocytes, the main route of TAG synthesis
AnswerC. Fatty acids → fatty acyl-CoA; glycerol 3-P → lysophosphatidic acid (GPAT) → phosphatidic acid (AGPAT) → DAG (phosphatidic acid phosphatase) → TAG (DGAT)
WhyThe first step is activation of fatty acids to fatty acyl-CoA (ATP); acyl groups are then added one at a time: GPAT makes lysophosphatidic acid, AGPAT phosphatidic acid, a phosphatase removes the phosphate to give DAG, and DGAT makes TAG. LPL breaks TAG down, and MGAT is the intestinal monoacylglycerol route.
Key factTAG synthesis order
  • Step 1: activate fatty acids: fatty acid → fatty acyl-CoA (fatty acyl-CoA synthetase, ATP).
  • Step 2: make glycerol 3-phosphate.
  • Step 3: acylate one at a time: G3P → lysophosphatidic acid (GPAT) → phosphatidic acid (AGPAT) → DAG (phosphatidic acid phosphatase) → TAG (DGAT). Intestine: 2-monoacylglycerol route via MGAT.
  • Regulation: insulin activates GPAT and MGAT by dephosphorylation (AMPK inhibits) and induces DGAT.
  • AGPAT (AGPAT2) deficiency → congenital generalized lipodystrophy: no adipose tissue, fatty liver.
The lecture figure (F1270:43) labels the first acylation MGAT; in liver and adipose it is GPAT. TA78 is the TA answer slide showing the pathway, not a separate stem.

WhyGlycerol kinase is absent in adipose, so adipocytes make glycerol 3-phosphate only by reducing glycolytic DHAP, which needs glucose entry by insulin-dependent GLUT4. Without insulin there is no backbone and no storage, while the liver uses both DHAP and glycerol kinase.
Key fact
  • Glycerol kinase (glycerol + ATP → glycerol 3-P): present in liver (and kidney), absent in adipose and muscle.

  • Liver (primary TAG-synthesis site): both routes, DHAP (GLUT2) and glycerol kinase.
  • Low insulin (type 1 diabetes) → no GLUT4 uptake → no glycerol 3-P → adipose cannot store TAG.
  • Glycerol kinase deficiency: very high glycerol in plasma and urine + fasting hypoglycemia (glycerol cannot enter gluconeogenesis).

Three hours after a fatty, carbohydrate-rich lunch, where do a woman's adipocytes get most of the fatty acids they store?
  1. A. Chylomicron TAG hydrolyzed by insulin-activated lipoprotein lipase on adipose capillaries
  2. B. LDL and HDL, unloaded by LCAT

AnswerA. Chylomicron TAG hydrolyzed by insulin-activated lipoprotein lipase on adipose capillaries
WhyAfter a meal dietary TAG arrives in chylomicrons (VLDL between meals), and insulin-induced lipoprotein lipase frees the fatty acids for re-esterification. HSL is the fasting lipase, adipose DNL is minor (the liver is the main site), and LDL/HDL carry mainly cholesterol.
Key fact
  • Liver = main site of de novo lipogenesis and the primary site of TAG synthesis; it stores little and exports TAG as VLDL. Excess glucose → liver fatty acids and TAG → VLDL → adipose.
  • Adipose = storage depot (over 95% of body TAG); its own DNL is minor. Fatty acids come from plasma: chylomicrons (post-prandial), VLDL (post-absorptive), or albumin-bound free fatty acids.
  • Lipoprotein TAG must first be hydrolyzed by lipoprotein lipase (capillary endothelium of adipose, muscle, heart).
  • Insulin: ↑ GLUT4, ↑ LPL, ↓ hormone-sensitive lipase → net TAG storage. HSL ↑ is a fasting event.

Fasting: releasing stored fat

During a 24-hour fast, a 30-year-old has rising plasma free fatty acids. Which change in the adipocyte best explains this?
  1. A. Increased lipoprotein lipase activity on adipose capillaries
  2. B. Glucagon directly hydrolyzing stored triacylglycerol
  3. C. Insulin-stimulated dephosphorylation of hormone-sensitive lipase
  4. D. Glucagon-stimulated rise in cAMP, PKA phosphorylation and activation of hormone-sensitive lipase
  5. E. Phosphodiesterase activation lowering cAMP, which activates hormone-sensitive lipase
AnswerD. Glucagon-stimulated rise in cAMP, PKA phosphorylation and activation of hormone-sensitive lipase
WhyGlucagon and epinephrine (β-receptors) raise cAMP → PKA, which phosphorylates and activates HSL; the freed fatty acids ride albumin. Lipoprotein lipase is the insulin-driven storage enzyme acting on circulating lipoprotein TAG, so it lowers, not raises, plasma FFA.
Key factHormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) releases fatty acids + glycerol from stored adipocyte TAG.
  • ON: glucagon, epinephrine/sympathetic drive (β-receptor) → ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylated = active HSL. Active in fasting, exercise, uncontrolled diabetes/DKA, ketogenic diet.
  • OFF: insulin (fed state, after a carbohydrate meal) → phosphodiesterase (↓cAMP) + protein phosphatase → dephosphorylated, inactive HSL.
  • Released fatty acids travel on serum albumin to liver and muscle.
  • Not lipoprotein lipase: insulin-induced, hydrolyzes chylomicron/VLDL TAG for storage (insulinoma → ↑LPL → ↓plasma FFA).
  • Insulin resistance → HSL no longer suppressed → ↑FFA → ↑liver TAG → ↑VLDL, ↓HDL.

In a fasting person, glycerol released from adipose tissue is turned into glucose in the liver. Which hepatic sequence is correct?
  1. A. Glycerol → pyruvate by pyruvate kinase → glucose
  2. B. Glycerol → acetyl-CoA → oxaloacetate → glucose
  3. C. Glycerol → glycerol 3-phosphate (glycerol kinase) → dihydroxyacetone phosphate → gluconeogenesis
  4. D. Glycerol → malonyl-CoA → glucose

WhyAdipocytes lack glycerol kinase, so glycerol goes to the liver, where glycerol kinase makes glycerol 3-phosphate and an NAD⁺-dependent dehydrogenase makes DHAP, a gluconeogenic triose. Routes through acetyl-CoA (B) never give net glucose.
Key fact
  • TAG lipolysis → fatty acids + glycerol. Glycerol is the only part of TAG that becomes glucose; even-chain fatty acids → acetyl-CoA → no net glucose.
  • Adipocytes lack glycerol kinase → glycerol travels to the liver: glycerol kinase (ATP) → glycerol 3-P → G3P dehydrogenase (needs NAD⁺) → DHAP → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate → glucose.
  • Alcohol: ↑NADH/NAD⁺ blocks G3P → DHAP → fasting hypoglycemia despite plenty of glycerol.
  • Ketogenic diet or long fast: glycerol (with glucogenic amino acids) becomes the glucose source.
  • Glycerol kinase deficiency → ↑free plasma glycerol → falsely high TAG on a glycerol-based assay.

  • β-Oxidation supports gluconeogenesis in two ways: it supplies ATP/NADH, and its acetyl-CoA regulates pyruvate.
  • Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase (mitochondrial, biotin + ATP, pyruvate → oxaloacetate, first gluconeogenic bypass) and inhibits PDH → pyruvate is carboxylated, not oxidized.
  • Acetyl-CoA is never a net glucose substrate; glycerol is the gluconeogenic carbon from fat.
  • Therefore any block in hepatic β-oxidation (MCAD, carnitine defects, ackee) → ↓gluconeogenesis → fasting hypoglycemia.

Carnitine shuttle and its control

124unlocks 8TA ×1
A long-chain fatty acyl-CoA has just been formed at the outer mitochondrial membrane. Which step comes next on its way into the matrix?
  1. A. CPT-2 transfers the acyl group from CoA to carnitine in the cytosol
  2. B. CPT-1 transfers the acyl group from CoA to carnitine
  3. C. Acyl-CoA synthetase in the matrix reactivates it
  4. D. It diffuses across the inner membrane without help
  5. E. The translocase transfers the acyl group back to CoA in the matrix
AnswerB. CPT-1 transfers the acyl group from CoA to carnitine
WhyCPT-1 (outer membrane) makes acylcarnitine, CACT carries it across the inner membrane, and CPT-2 (inner membrane) returns the acyl group to CoA in the matrix. Long-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner membrane on its own; only short and medium chains can.
Key fact
  • Phase I: activation to acyl-CoA in the cytosol (acyl-CoA synthetase on the ER, outer mitochondrial and peroxisomal membranes), then the shuttle.
  • CPT-1 (outer membrane): acyl group from CoA → carnitine. CACT: swaps acylcarnitine across the inner membrane. CPT-2 (inner membrane): acyl group back to CoA in the matrix.
  • Short and medium chains cross the inner membrane without carnitine.
  • Carnitine: mainly diet (meat); limited synthesis in liver and kidney from lysine + SAM; heart and skeletal muscle make none (high-affinity uptake). Vegans/vegetarians → low carnitine.
  • Too little carnitine → CPT-1 can't form acylcarnitine → long-chain fatty acids can't be oxidized.

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Vegan or vegetarian with muscle weakness → main carnitine source (meat) / mechanism (can't move long chains into mitochondria)
  • Which enzyme 'transports fatty acids into the mitochondria' (CPT-1)

What it lets you eliminate

  • Short and medium chains do not need the shuttle; long chains always do
  • CPT-2 acts on the matrix side (acylcarnitine → acyl-CoA), never in the cytosol
  • The body does not 'make its own' carnitine in heart or muscle

Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of fatty acid oxidation, and where is it located?
  1. A. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1, outer mitochondrial membrane
  2. B. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, cytosol

  5. E. Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase, inner mitochondrial membrane
AnswerA. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1, outer mitochondrial membrane
WhyCPT-1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane is rate-limiting for fatty acid oxidation and is where malonyl-CoA acts. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, the usual trap.
Key fact
  • CPT-1 = rate-limiting step of fatty acid oxidation, located on the outer mitochondrial membrane.
  • Inhibited by malonyl-CoA, the product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), so newly made fatty acids are not burned as they are made.
  • Pair: ACC = rate-limiting for synthesis (citrate activates it); CPT-1 = rate-limiting for oxidation (malonyl-CoA inhibits it).
  • So the ACC product modulates fatty acid transport into mitochondria, not 'degradation in the cytosol'.

Shortly after a large carbohydrate meal, insulin rises. What happens to hepatic fatty acid oxidation, and why?
  1. A. It decreases, because insulin activates hormone-sensitive lipase
  2. B. It decreases, because insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, raising malonyl-CoA, which inhibits CPT-1
  3. C. It increases, because insulin dephosphorylates acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
  4. D. It increases, because insulin activates CPT-1 directly
  5. E. It decreases, because insulin lowers malonyl-CoA
AnswerB. It decreases, because insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, raising malonyl-CoA, which inhibits CPT-1
WhyInsulin turns ACC on → ↑malonyl-CoA → CPT-1 inhibited → ↓β-oxidation. Glucagon, epinephrine and AMP (AMPK) do the reverse: ACC off, malonyl-CoA falls, CPT-1 opens and β-oxidation rises.
Key factACC sets the malonyl-CoA level, and malonyl-CoA sets CPT-1.
  • Insulin (fed) and citrate → ACC on → ↑malonyl-CoA → CPT-1 off → ↓fatty acid oxidation.
  • Glucagon/epinephrine (PKA phosphorylates ACC) and AMP/AMPK (exercise, low energy) → ACC off (AMP also speeds malonyl-CoA breakdown) → ↓malonyl-CoA → CPT-1 on → ↑fatty acid oxidation (and, in liver, ketogenesis).
  • Bottom line: glucagon/epinephrine ↑FA oxidation; insulin ↓FA oxidation.
  • Loss of muscle ACC2 → no malonyl-CoA brake → unregulated FA oxidation and weight loss. Von Gierke disease: extra glycolysis → citrate → malonyl-CoA → CPT-1 shut → ketones do not rise.

Each turn of mitochondrial β-oxidation of palmitoyl-CoA follows which sequence, giving which products?
  1. A. Oxidation (FAD) → hydration → oxidation (NAD⁺) → thiolysis; 1 FADH₂, 1 NADH, 1 acetyl-CoA
  2. B. Condensation → reduction → dehydration → reduction; uses NADPH
  3. C. Thiolysis → oxidation → hydration → dehydration; 1 FADH₂ only
  4. D. Hydration → oxidation → thiolysis → oxidation; 2 NADH
  5. E. Oxidation (NAD⁺) → dehydration → oxidation (FAD) → thiolysis; 1 NADH, 1 acetyl-CoA
AnswerA. Oxidation (FAD) → hydration → oxidation (NAD⁺) → thiolysis; 1 FADH₂, 1 NADH, 1 acetyl-CoA
WhyEach cycle is dehydrogenation (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, FAD) → hydration → dehydrogenation (NAD⁺) → thiolysis, giving 1 FADH₂ + 1 NADH + 1 acetyl-CoA. Condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction with NADPH is fatty acid synthesis.
Key fact
  • Phase II cycle: oxidation → hydration → oxidation → thiolysis (dehydrogenation, hydration, dehydrogenation, thiolysis).
  • Step 1: chain-length-specific acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (SCAD, MCAD, LCAD, VLCAD), FAD → FADH₂; its electrons pass to ETF → ETF:CoQ oxidoreductase → CoQ (lose that and step 1 stalls).
  • Step 3: 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase → NADH. Step 4: thiolase releases acetyl-CoA + an acyl-CoA 2 carbons shorter.
  • Each cycle = 1 FADH₂, 1 NADH, 1 acetyl-CoA.
  • Synthesis runs the opposite logic: condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction (NADPH, cytosol).

Which statement about the pathways of fatty acid oxidation is correct?
  1. A. Unsaturated fatty acids are oxidized only in peroxisomes
  2. B. ω-Oxidation occurs in peroxisomes and is the main route for phytanic acid
  3. C. Oxidation of fatty acids longer than C20 begins in mitochondria

  5. E. ω-Oxidation in mitochondria releases acetyl-CoA from the β-carbon

Whyα-oxidation = peroxisome, phytanic acid, no energy. ω-oxidation is in the ER (cytochrome P450) and makes dicarboxylic acids; very long chains start in peroxisomes; unsaturated fats use mitochondrial β-oxidation plus two extra enzymes.
Key fact
  • β-oxidation: mitochondria of liver and muscle; major pathway for chains below C20; oxidizes the β-carbon → acetyl-CoA.
  • Peroxisomal β-oxidation: VLCFA above C20; less energy than mitochondria.
  • α-oxidation: peroxisomes; branched phytanic acid; minor, no energy yield.
  • ω-oxidation: ER (cytochrome P450); minor (lecture: normally SCFA below C6); makes dicarboxylic acids; rises when β-oxidation fails (MCAD).
  • Unsaturated: mitochondrial β-oxidation plus enoyl-CoA isomerase and an NADPH-dependent reductase → fewer ATP (a bond at an odd position skips one FADH₂; at an even position it also costs NADPH).
Lecture slide F1278:7 says ω-oxidation substrates are normally SCFA below C6 (textbooks say C10–C12); course wording kept.

  • Primary carnitine deficiency (carnitine transporter, diet/vegan, synthesis, renal reabsorption): ↓free carnitine + ↓acylcarnitines, ↑FFA, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, fatty liver, muscle cramps and weakness.

  • So the acylcarnitine level separates carnitine deficiency (low) from CPT-2 deficiency (high long-chain species).
  • CPT-2 (muscle form): exercise- or fast-induced myalgia, rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuria, ↑CK, cardiomyopathy. CPT-1 or CACT defects: lethal young.
  • Treatment of shuttle defects: high-carb/low long-chain fat, add medium-chain fat (bypasses carnitine), carnitine supplements, limit exertion.

In prolonged fasting, hepatic β-oxidation is high but citric acid cycle flux is low. Why does acetyl-CoA go to ketone bodies?
  1. A. Insulin activates ketogenesis
  2. B. Excess glucose is converted into ketones
  3. C. Acetyl-CoA is low, so the liver stores it as ketones
  4. D. The liver needs ketones as its own main fuel
  5. E. Oxaloacetate is pulled into gluconeogenesis and high NADH slows the cycle, so acetyl-CoA exceeds TCA capacity
AnswerE. Oxaloacetate is pulled into gluconeogenesis and high NADH slows the cycle, so acetyl-CoA exceeds TCA capacity
WhyFasting and type 1 diabetes flood the liver with fatty acids; oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis and NADH from β-oxidation inhibits the TCA dehydrogenases, so excess acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria becomes ketone bodies for other tissues.
Key fact
  • ↑Lipolysis (fasting, type 1 diabetes) → ↑fatty acids to liver → ↑β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA + ↑NADH.
  • Oxaloacetate drained into gluconeogenesis (↑PC, PEPCK); NADH inhibits the TCA dehydrogenases → the cycle can't take the acetyl-CoA.
  • Excess acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria → ketone bodies, made from fatty acids, not glucose.
  • Purpose: water-soluble fuel for brain and muscle; the liver itself can't use them.
  • Fat's end product is acetyl-CoA, hence the name 'ketogenic' diet.

A person with alcoholic ketoacidosis has a very high hepatic mitochondrial NADH/NAD⁺ ratio. Which change in ketone body metabolism follows?
  1. A. More acetone is made by an NADH-dependent enzyme
  2. B. HMG-CoA lyase is inhibited by NADH

  5. E. Thiophorase is induced in the liver
AnswerD. More acetoacetate is reduced to β-hydroxybutyrate, which becomes the dominant ketone
Whyβ-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase uses NADH to reduce acetoacetate, so a high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio (DKA, alcohol, long fast) shifts the pair toward β-hydroxybutyrate. Acetone forms spontaneously, and the liver never has thiophorase.
Key fact
  • Acetoacetate + NADH ⇌ β-hydroxybutyrate + NAD⁺ (β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase).
  • High NADH/NAD⁺ (β-oxidation in DKA, ethanol oxidation, prolonged fasting) → more β-hydroxybutyrate; ketone production rises, not falls, as NADH/NAD⁺ rises.
  • β-Hydroxybutyrate is the main circulating ketone (after 5 weeks of starvation about 6 mM, several-fold above acetoacetate) and the main brain fuel in a long fast.
  • Alcoholic ketoacidosis: ↑NADH → ↑β-hydroxybutyrate, and oxaloacetate/pyruvate → malate/lactate → hypoglycemia.

Which enzyme allows heart muscle to oxidize acetoacetate but is absent from the liver?
  1. A. β-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase
  2. B. Succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase)
  3. C. HMG-CoA lyase
  4. D. Glucose 6-phosphatase
  5. E. Acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase
AnswerB. Succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase)
WhyExtrahepatic tissues activate acetoacetate with thiophorase, taking CoA from succinyl-CoA, and thiolase splits acetoacetyl-CoA into 2 acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle. The liver lacks thiophorase, so it makes ketones but can't use them; it does have β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase and thiolase.
Key fact
  • Ketolysis (brain, heart, skeletal muscle, kidney): β-hydroxybutyrate → acetoacetate (β-HB dehydrogenase) → thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase; CoA donor = succinyl-CoA) → acetoacetyl-CoA → thiolase → 2 acetyl-CoA → TCA.
  • Ketone bodies are a water-soluble fuel (no albumin needed).
  • Liver lacks thiophorase → makes but cannot use ketone bodies and exports them; it fuels itself by β-oxidation of fatty acids.
  • Thiophorase missing in peripheral tissues too → can't make acetoacetyl-CoA from acetoacetate → recurrent ketoacidosis.
  • Lecture yield: acetoacetate 23 ATP, β-hydroxybutyrate 26 ATP.

A person has had only water for 3 weeks and is alert. Which fuel pattern best fits?
  1. A. Brain gets much of its energy from ketone bodies; RBCs still use glucose and make lactate
  2. B. Liver oxidizes ketone bodies; muscle uses only glucose
  3. C. Liver glycogenolysis supplies most blood glucose
  4. D. Brain oxidizes fatty acids; RBCs oxidize ketone bodies
  5. E. Brain still runs entirely on glucose
AnswerA. Brain gets much of its energy from ketone bodies; RBCs still use glucose and make lactate
WhyIn a prolonged fast ketones rise enough for the brain to switch to ketone bodies (mostly β-hydroxybutyrate), cutting its glucose need and sparing muscle protein. RBCs have no mitochondria, so they use glucose → lactate; the brain can't burn fatty acids; the liver can't use ketones; glycogen is gone within about a day.
Key factWho burns what
  • Brain: glucose when fed and early in fasting; never fatty acids (they barely cross the blood–brain barrier); ketone bodies in prolonged fasting (most of its energy by about 3–4 weeks) → less gluconeogenesis from amino acids → muscle protein spared, urea output falls.
  • RBCs: no mitochondria → glucose only → lactate.
  • Liver: glycogenolysis early (stores gone by about 24–36 h), then gluconeogenesis + ketogenesis; fuels itself with fatty acids, not ketones.
  • Muscle: fatty acids and ketones; sends alanine/glutamine for gluconeogenesis. Heart: prefers fatty acids (palmitate) even when fed.
  • Fatty acid oxidation happens only in the mitochondrial matrix.

  • Glucagon acts on liver and adipose (gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, ketogenesis), not muscle protein breakdown (muscle has no glucagon receptors).

  • 'Glucagon does NOT do…' (muscle protein breakdown); glucagon in prolonged fasting → ↑ketogenesis; PEPCK induced
  • Multi-select: glucagon ↑lipolysis, ↑NADH, ↑acetyl-CoA

What it lets you eliminate

  • In insulin deficiency, FAS, ACC, glucokinase, glycogen synthase and GLUT4 are never 'more active'
  • ↑glycolysis or ↓FA oxidation are the wrong arrows in DKA
  • Glucagon never decreases lipolysis or raises insulin

Diabetic ketoacidosis

144unlocks 10
A 12-year-old has polyuria, vomiting, deep rapid breathing and fruity breath; glucose is 480 mg/dL. Which finding is expected?
  1. A. Metabolic alkalosis
  2. B. High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with urine acetoacetate
  3. C. Normal anion gap
  4. D. Hypervolemia
  5. E. Low serum β-hydroxybutyrate
AnswerB. High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with urine acetoacetate
WhyAcetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are acids (pKa 3.5) that release H⁺ at blood pH → high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul breathing and ketonuria. Acetone, formed spontaneously from acetoacetate, gives the fruity breath. Osmotic diuresis causes volume loss, not hypervolemia.
Key fact
  • Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are organic acids (pKa 3.5) → H⁺ load → ↑anion gap metabolic acidosis, ↓HCO₃⁻, Kussmaul respiration (respiratory compensation).
  • Acetone: non-enzymatic from acetoacetate, not an acid, not a fuel, exhaled → fruity breath.
  • DKA labs: hyperglycemia + glucosuria, ↑serum β-hydroxybutyrate, urine ketones (acetoacetate), ↑anion gap, dehydration, low C-peptide in type 1.
  • Insulin treatment stops lipolysis and ketogenesis; ketoacids are burned and HCO₃⁻ regenerated → pH rises; glucose and serum K⁺ fall.
  • Nutritional (physiologic) ketosis: ketones up modestly, pH stays normal.
q1386 keys 'bicarbonate solution is a treatment staple' for DKA; standard care is isotonic saline, insulin and K⁺, with bicarbonate only for severe acidosis. Not counted.
What it unlocks: 10 questions · 3 you might not expect

Questions you might not expect it to answer (3)

  1. Trap: the obvious answer is wrongQ1659 Long DKA case: which statement about ketone bodies is correct (glucose origin, liver use, acetoacetate fruity odor, albumin carrier, organic acids)?
    'Acetoacetate gives fruity breath' is the trap: the odor is acetone. Ketones come from fat, the liver can't use them, and need no albumin. Answer: organic acids adding to the proton load.
  2. Vignette never names itQ1337Q1575 5-year-old with vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, stupor and glucose 270: which lab abnormality will be found?
    Diabetes is never mentioned; hyperglycemia + Kussmaul breathing + vomiting = new-onset DKA. Expect increased serum β-hydroxybutyrate; pH falls, the gap rises and the child is volume depleted, so the other options flip.
  3. Vignette never names itQ1584 5-year-old with vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, confusion and glucose 270: which lab abnormality will be found?
    Recognize unnamed DKA. Insulin lack drives ketogenesis, so increased serum β-hydroxybutyrate; expect acidemia, a high anion gap and hypovolemia rather than the listed opposites.

How it shows up

  • Child with vomiting, rapid breathing and high glucose → which lab (↑β-hydroxybutyrate)
  • New-onset type 1 diabetes with fruity breath and urine reducing sugar → ↑urine acetoacetate
  • Hallmark of ketoacidosis (fruity breath)
  • An insulin injection in untreated type 1 diabetes increases what (blood pH)
  • Ketone bodies are organic acids adding to the proton load; physiologic ketosis keeps pH normal

What it lets you eliminate

  • Normal anion gap, alkalosis, hypervolemia and low glucose don't fit DKA
  • The fruity odor is acetone, not acetoacetate
  • Ketones don't need albumin; insulin lowers (not raises) serum K⁺ and glucose

MCAD deficiency (Helga)

A 7-month-old is unrousable after a viral illness with poor feeding. Glucose is low, urine ketones are absent, plasma octanoylcarnitine (C8) is high, and urine has medium-chain dicarboxylic acids. Which step is most directly defective?
  1. A. α-Oxidation of branched fatty acids
  2. B. Peroxisomal oxidation of fatty acids longer than C20
  3. C. Ketone body synthesis by HMG-CoA synthase
  4. D. The first, FAD-linked oxidation of β-oxidation for C6–C12 acyl-CoAs
  5. E. Carnitine uptake into cells
AnswerD. The first, FAD-linked oxidation of β-oxidation for C6–C12 acyl-CoAs
WhyHypoketotic hypoglycemia after a fast + ↑C6–C10 (C8) acylcarnitines + dicarboxylic aciduria = MCAD deficiency, the medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (first oxidation, C6–C12) of mitochondrial β-oxidation. Carnitine-uptake defects give low acylcarnitines; ketogenesis falls only secondarily.
Key fact
  • MCAD = medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, first FAD-linked step of mitochondrial β-oxidation for C6–C12 (SCAD below C6, LCAD C14–C18, VLCAD above C20). Most common fatty acid oxidation disorder (about 1 in 12,000; Northern European ancestry).
  • Fingerprint: infant or toddler, fasting or illness (vomiting, poor feeding) → lethargy or coma, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly with fatty liver, ↑ammonia, ↑anion gap, ↑C6–C10 acylcarnitines (C8), dicarboxylic aciduria, hexanoyl- and suberylglycine; sibling with a Reye-like death.
  • 'Mom couldn't wake her' = hypoglycemia (the brain has neither glucose nor ketones).
  • Differential for hypoketotic hypoglycemia: carnitine, CPT and LCAD defects, congenital hyperinsulinism (no acylcarnitine rise), Reye syndrome.
What it unlocks: 27 questions · 1 you might not expect

Questions you might not expect it to answer (1)

  1. Answered by eliminationQ1616 3-month-old unresponsive after poor feeding with an ear infection: glucose 45, no ketones, normal acylcarnitine, unusual carboxylic acids: which enzyme?
    Normal acylcarnitines seem to argue against MCAD, but the unusual acids are dicarboxylic (ω-oxidation), which shuttle defects never produce. With hypoketotic hypoglycemia after illness: MCAD.

How it shows up

  • Helga case: most likely diagnosis from the lab table (hypoketotic hypoglycemia, probably MCAD)
  • Short vignette: overnight fast, low ketones, ↑acylcarnitines and dicarboxylic acids → enzyme
  • Which pathway is most directly affected (β-oxidation of C6–C12 fatty acids)
  • Why mom couldn't wake her (hypoglycemia); which labs are abnormal (all)
  • C8–C10 acylcarnitines → MCAD rather than SCAD, VLCAD, CPT-2 or CACT

What it lets you eliminate

  • 'Hyperketotic', hyperglycemia, increased gluconeogenesis or more ketone use are the opposite of MCAD
  • OTC, PDH and primary carnitine deficiency don't give C8 acylcarnitines with dicarboxylic acids
  • α-oxidation, peroxisomal oxidation, palmitate synthesis and ketone synthesis are the wrong pathway
  • Metabolic alkalosis, sleep apnea and aspiration don't explain the stupor

In MCAD deficiency, which pair of hepatic changes explains both the fasting hypoglycemia and the low ketones?
  1. A. ↓ glycogen phosphorylase activity and excess stored glycogen
  2. B. ↓ ATP and ↑ acetyl-CoA
  3. C. ↓ ATP and ↓ acetyl-CoA
  4. D. ↑ ATP and ↑ acetyl-CoA
  5. E. ↑ insulin and ↓ glucagon
AnswerC. ↓ ATP and ↓ acetyl-CoA
WhyBlocked β-oxidation yields less acetyl-CoA (the substrate for ketogenesis and the obligatory activator of pyruvate carboxylase) and less ATP to run gluconeogenesis. Once glycogen runs out, ketones and glucose both fall; insulin and glycogen handling are normal.
Key fact
  • MCAD block → ↓ATP and ↓acetyl-CoA in the fasting liver.
  • Hypoglycemia: gluconeogenesis needs ATP, and acetyl-CoA is the obligatory allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase → ↓gluconeogenesis. Tissues that can't burn fat use more glucose, illness raises needs, and an overnight fast empties glycogen (↑glucose demand, ↓gluconeogenesis).
  • Hypoketosis: low acetyl-CoA = low ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate).
  • Same logic for any hepatic β-oxidation block (carnitine, CPT-1, ackee): hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
What it unlocks: 30 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Toddler, poor intake, ↑C8 acylcarnitine → mechanism of hypoglycemia (↓ATP, ↓pyruvate carboxylase activation)
  • Case short answers: account for the hypoglycemia; account for the hypoketosis
  • MCQ: fasting hypoglycemia is a consequence of ↓acetyl-CoA production; 'reduced gluconeogenesis due to low ATP and low acetyl-CoA'
  • Lethargic between feedings: ↑glucose demand but ↓gluconeogenesis; 'insufficient energy for gluconeogenesis'

What it lets you eliminate

  • Excess insulin, glycogen storage defects and poor glucose absorption are not the cause
  • 'Decreased ability to convert acetyl-CoA to glucose' is a trap: acetyl-CoA never makes net glucose anyway
  • No acylcarnitine or dicarboxylic acid inhibition of gluconeogenesis; the problem is too little energy and activator
  • The gluconeogenic enzymes themselves are intact

An infant in an MCAD crisis has plasma ammonia of 100 µmol/L (normal below 20). Which mechanism best explains it?
  1. A. Dicarboxylic acids activating glutaminase
  2. B. Excess dietary protein
  3. C. Ketone bodies inhibiting carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
  4. D. Accumulated octanoate uncouples mitochondria, lowering the ATP the urea cycle needs
  5. E. Inherited ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
AnswerD. Accumulated octanoate uncouples mitochondria, lowering the ATP the urea cycle needs
WhyAccumulated octanoic acid (C8) is a mitochondrial toxin that uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, and the fatty liver works poorly, so hepatic ATP falls and the ATP-hungry urea cycle slows. Ketones are low in MCAD, so D can't be right.
Key fact
  • MCAD → medium chains (octanoate, C8) accumulate → uncouple oxidative phosphorylation → ↓ATP → ↓urea synthesis → hyperammonemia.
  • Fatty infiltration also diminishes liver function.
  • So MCAD = ↓fatty acid oxidation + ↓urea synthesis + ↑ammonia (never ↓ammonia).
Course case answer is octanoate uncoupling → ↓ATP → ↓urea cycle; the N-acetylglutamate/CPS-I mechanism some sources add is a textbook extra.

The urine of a child with MCAD deficiency contains suberylglycine, a conjugate of a C8 dicarboxylic acid. Where does the dicarboxylic acid come from?
  1. A. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
  2. B. ω-Oxidation of backed-up fatty acids by cytochrome P450 in the endoplasmic reticulum
  3. C. Peroxisomal VLCFA transport
  4. D. Peroxisomal α-oxidation
  5. E. Ketone body breakdown
AnswerB. ω-Oxidation of backed-up fatty acids by cytochrome P450 in the endoplasmic reticulum
WhyMedium-chain acyl groups MCAD can't oxidize leave as C6–C10 acylcarnitines or glycine conjugates (hexanoylglycine, C6); some go through ER ω-oxidation (P450) to dicarboxylic acids (suberate, C8 → suberylglycine). These unmeasured acids, not ketones, raise the anion gap.
Key fact
  • Medium-chain acyl-CoA trapped in mitochondria → carnitine acyltransferases → leave as C6, C8, C10 acylcarnitines (blood) or free acids.
  • Hexanoylglycine = C6 monocarboxylic glycine conjugate (β-oxidation intermediate).
  • Suberylglycine = C8 dicarboxylic conjugate from ω-oxidation (ER, cytochrome P450), which increases whenever β-oxidation fails.
  • Anion gap ↑ (20 vs 8–16) from accumulated mono- and dicarboxylic acids, not ketones (ketones are low).
  • Carnitine synthesis, transport and acyltransferases are normal.

What it lets you eliminate

  • In MCAD the gap is not from ketones
  • α-oxidation, methylmalonyl-CoA and VLCFA transport are unrelated

Which test best confirms a suspected diagnosis of MCAD deficiency?
  1. A. ACADM gene analysis (common European Lys304Glu) and/or MCAD activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts
  2. B. Urine ketone dipstick
  3. C. Brain MRI
  4. D. Liver ultrasound
  5. E. Fasting blood glucose
AnswerA. ACADM gene analysis (common European Lys304Glu) and/or MCAD activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts
WhyConfirmation is genetic analysis of ACADM (chromosome 1); the common European mutation Lys304Glu (K304E, 985A→G) impairs assembly of the MCAD homotetramer. MCAD activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts supports it; glucose and ketones only raise suspicion.
Key fact
  • Gene: ACADM (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, medium chain), chromosome 1; MCAD is a homotetramer.
  • Most common mutation in people of European descent: Lys304Glu (K304E), 985A→G → impaired tetramer assembly.
  • Biochemical support: MCAD enzyme activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts; β-oxidation in cultured fibroblasts (C6–C10 acylcarnitines).
  • Imaging, glucose and urine ketones do not confirm it.

Which instruction is appropriate for the parent of an infant with MCAD deficiency?
  1. A. Use a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet
  2. B. Allow a 12-hour overnight fast
  3. C. Use a formula rich in medium-chain triglycerides
  4. D. Start a high-fat ketogenic diet
  5. E. Feed every 3–4 hours with complex carbohydrate, avoid fasting, and give extra glucose during illness
AnswerE. Feed every 3–4 hours with complex carbohydrate, avoid fasting, and give extra glucose during illness
WhyMCAD patients can't burn fat in a fast, so management is avoid fasting: frequent complex-carbohydrate feeds, lower fat, uncooked cornstarch at bedtime later, extra glucose when ill. MCT formulas are contraindicated because medium chains need MCAD; MCT is for carnitine-shuttle defects.
Key fact
  • Avoid fasting; frequent feeds (every 3–4 h) with complex carbohydrates; extra or IV glucose during illness or vomiting.
  • Avoid medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) formulas.
  • As a toddler: relatively low-fat diet (under 30% of calories) and uncooked cornstarch (2 g/kg) at bedtime for slow overnight glucose.
  • Carnitine supplements may replace carnitine lost as acylcarnitines.
  • Ketogenic, high-fat, high-protein/low-carb diets, fasting and glucagon all provoke crises.
